utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce to the Chamber Joaquim Gaye, who is from France and is working as an intern during this term in our office. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just one quick matter. The Court has raised a scheduling possibility concerning the week of the 9th through the 13th. As it turns out, I'm the one who has a previous commitment. I should have remembered it at the time with -- actually, with the ICC. So that would present a problem for me. Let me say quickly that if it's a matter of my being present versus a member of the Bench, then by all means I'll make whatever arrangements are necessary and we should not -- we shouldn't sit pursuant to 15 bis unnecessarily. But if it's simply another matter that doesn't implicate someone's presence, then I would of course prefer to be here all four days. So I leave it to the Court with that information, I'm otherwise previously committed on Friday, but I don't believe I have a witness at that time so my absence can be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your kindness is very much appreciated. We'll sit from 10th to 13th in that week. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when we adjourned we were discussing the meeting of November 8th, 1992, that's P1481, and if we could turn to page 147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have some technical difficulties. Shall we take a short break. Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. --- Break taken at 9.05 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope it is okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then we should begin by again calling up P1481 at page 147.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we discussed before we adjourned the portion of this discussion that related to the "ciscenje" of the Drina, but you mentioned at that meeting two pressing tasks, not only "ciscenje" of the Drina but that the -- also stated that the most pressing thing is to "ociste" Orasje. Now, you mentioned Orasje once or twice here in this court in passing, but the subject of Orasje also came up during your trial, correct, and your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, for the -- Orasje was a municipality in northern Bosnia that was about 80 per cent non-Serb, that is, it was a vastly majority non-Serb municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could call up 65 ter 00242Q.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's a reflection of the demographics of Orasje with vast predominance of Croats and Serbs comprising about 19 per cent or so of the population; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that is true. I don't know the exact figures, but Orasje was mostly populated by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the context in which Orasje came up in your trial was in connection with questions regarding what you had said in a broadcast where you were standing in front of an ethnic map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could have -- I tender the 65 ter 00242Q, the census, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6519, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So in your trial there were -- there was a point at which you were asked questions about what you had said in connection with an ethnic map, and we can -- that video is in evidence in this case and I'd like to show you a quick still of that, 65 ter 25658. All right. Now, that's a still taken from what is in evidence in this case and what was shown in your case, P797, which begins with you saying: "We are standing in front of an ethnic map of former Bosnia and Herzegovina with marked borders of the territory that is presently possessed by the Bosnian Serb army. I can only say that what was being said, that we are possessing the territories ethnically populated by the other national communities, that is not true, as can be seen on the ethnic man of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which we can cover with a transparent sheet on which the territories are exactly marked which is possessed by our army, that those are in fact areas that belong to our people." Now, the Presiding Judge asked you some questions at that point and he noted that at one -- and now we're referring to transcript pages 25645 and 25646 in your case. He noted that you had said that, although this vast horseshoe area represented in the blue/green represented the areas possessed by your army, the areas that you said were in fact areas that belonged to our people, that there was a smaller area that's not yet held by our forces. I mean, it's not liberated yet, that is Orasje. And the Judge asked you to point to Orasje. And you said: "Oh, Orasje is Croatian. There's no problem there. That wasn't the correct statement on my part." You said Orasje was Croatian along the Sava River and "you're quite right, we didn't have the right to Orasje." That's what you told Judge Orie. And you [sic] said: "Yes, but you said: It still has to be liberated." And you said: "Yes, I did." You pointed out -- and you said: "But I wasn't right there. I wasn't right on that score." Now, first of all, that's a correct summary, is it not, of the exchange that took place in your trial between you and Judge Orie in connection with this ethnic map and the issue of Orasje?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you have raised a complex issue regarding the map, but I will come to the map later. I suppose and I believe that it is true that this exchange took place as you described, but it was a similar exchange to the one that I mentioned last time --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- when I presented to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, excuse me, sorry. You posed a complex question to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, the question was rather complex. Let him continue. Let's see what he's up to. Please continue, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I have to object. Mr. Tieger wants to achieve a goal by posing wrong questions without going into details --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. That's not correct observation. He's entitled to put his case. He's entitled to put any questions. Please try to answer the question and we'll give you an opportunity to explain further, if necessary. The question was mainly about Orasje, your position --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I may, Mr. President. The question was simply whether or not that's what he said under oath when he testified previously. So that part is fairly simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He confirmed that and he wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that, but I just wanted to clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. You're right. I said that I don't doubt that the record is correct. I don't remember all the details, though, but I do remember the map. This is a complex issue and every answer that I give would be incomplete unless I give you a thorough explanation. That was the only comment that I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that explanation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you confirm that it is your mistake to refer to Orasje as a smaller area to be liberated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't my mistake. I rather gave a wrong answer. I don't know to date whether this is correct, what is stated in Mr. Mladic's diary. I didn't say that Orasje needs to be liberated and that I'm showing on the map that Orasje should belong to the Croats, and I never entertained an opinion that the Serbian army should take hold of the area, that according to our maps and the plan and the agreement with the Croatian side should belong to the Croatian side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, your comment about Orasje was broadcast in TV Pale. You see, this is a -- you see yourself in front of map, that's a video -- part of the video conveying your statement. In that statement you are said to have commented that Orasje should be liberated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I would kindly ask the part of the statement to be read out, the one that accompanies this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we play that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the interpreters have the transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be the best approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's only one-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or we can print it out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The booths don't have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can give them a hard copy if you want to run it up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be coming. The Registry could print it out in a minute. Mr. Krajisnik, are you happy to read this transcript or would you like to hear the sound -- the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it would be enough for me to read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you can see it -- you can see the word "Orasje" on line 32, if that's of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. You said it in the video; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this video I would like to explain what I meant regarding Orasje. I'll start with this part that deals with the proximity of Orasje. The territory of Republika Srpska is actually represented by the border along the Una river, the Sava River, with a smaller area that is not yet under our forces. I mean, it is not liberated yet, that is Orasje. That is the border of Semberija, et cetera. Then further on, it's the territory of Semberija, territory of Ozren, and territory of eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina. We presented as our territory to the Croatian community in Graz, and so on and so forth. Namely, one can see here -- perhaps it's just a problem of comprehension. I'm saying that we are looking at the border that was being held by our forces, so maybe it was not the happiest way of formulating the phrase to liberate Orasje. What I meant was that Orasje was there in the part where our forces were not on the Sava, but I made reference to the talks that we had with the Croats in Graz when we said that, generally speaking, there should be a corridor and that by exchange of territories we could have part of Posavina populated by Croats. This is not an invitation nor a claim to Croatian territories. This is rather an implicit indication that we did discuss Semberija and Posavina with the Croats in Graz, and, now, when I'm showing the map, I say that our goal is the Sava, whereas at present we are still not holding the territory or the part of territory with Orasje in it. This should never be interpreted in that way. Maybe it was not put in a correct way, meaning that we should occupy it militarily. I was just pointing to the map and to the fact that there is a place called Orasje there that was not under the control of our forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you said in this broadcast, referring to areas that had been taken by and were held by the VRS, that this is what was possessed with one exception, Orasje, that had not yet been liberated. You pressed on November 8th for the VRS to "ociste" Orasje, and you continued -- you and Dr. Karadzic continued to press for the duration of the war for the VRS to take Orasje, which had not been successfully taken and were still doing so in 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for sure the army tried to reach the Sava River. In the end that was the military plan that one should not have enemy forces behind one's back when we're talking about the corridor. But this is already a stage of the war when large territories, Serbian territories, fell under somebody else's command and then it was normal that everybody at the local level tried to expand the territories of their own ethnic community. But that was not what you say, that it was an instruction. I'm just going to remind you of your own conversation. You mentioned that last time we did brief Mr. Adzic on the 6th and 7th of May and Mr. Mladic as well, this is what you said, discussing the strategic goals. Then the JNA held Neretva and an exit to the sea, and what happened? Just a few days later the Yugoslav army withdrew. The local army --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, stop. We're still talking about Orasje. You've just said -- apparently the answer to my question is no. You didn't continue to press for the VRS to take Orasje, but that locals may have done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I'd like to turn to P1473, at English page 130 through 131 and B/C/S 132 to 133 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to be more precise, please. This is not what I said. I need to make a slight correction. What I said at the end of the war when the territories began to be captured outside of what we had talked about it and agreed with the Croats in Graz, then a large number of the territories belonging to the other ethnic community were in question. And then of course, as far as Orasje is concerned, the army wanted to clear that area, to capture it militarily, so as not to have soldiers behind their backs in relation to the corridor. So these are all these situations in which the war was waged. I didn't say that there were conversations where Orasje should be taken. It was simply a question of securing the corridor, and then again in talks these things would be resolved politically and not through the military situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The document in front of us now, P1473, at page 130, reflects a meeting between General Mladic and President Milosevic, General Perisic, and General Gvero. As we can see at the beginning, President Milosevic states that he received Mr. Karadzic and you, Mr. Krajisnik, the day earlier. They said bad things about you and also attacked Gvero. Milosevic notes: "It is my impression that Krajisnik is normal but stupid. Karadzic is overburdened with history, he's not normal. They live in a kind of historic fantasy world ..." He goes on to say -- to claim that: "There is no military solution for the crisis in Yugoslavia ...," pressing for a political solution. And then observes: "They," still referring to you and Mr. Karadzic, "say that they should seize Orasje." And he says: "You cannot keep 70 per cent of the territory." If we move to the next page, he then discusses what he wants to present in connection with the negotiations, and then continues toward the bottom of the page. There was clearly a discussion about those negotiations with you and Mr. Karadzic. And then he says: "Moma," apparently referring to you, "wrote it down, but we'll see what they will do. They are carried away by the idea of seizing Orasje. "I don't think Radovan will accept; he is a bad student of history and he's in some sort of poetic fervour." Now, that, Mr. Krajisnik, is a reflection of your continuing focus on Orasje which began in 1992, was reflected in the broadcast that we saw, in the meeting of 8 November, in directive 4, and now continuing on into 1995.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the map does not date from 1992. If you can see, you can see that in the eastern part there were no enclaves which did exist. This is probably a map from 1995 or 1994. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I don't know now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you acknowledge in your own case, and I'll find the reference, but maybe you can confirm, if you -- if you remember, that you acknowledge that map as from 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map is not from 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The map and the broadcast. I'll find you the reference and then you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please find my written objection to you where I said that this is not a map from 1992. If you look at the map, you'll see that there were no enclaves on it, no Srebrenica, no Zepa, and they did exist -- they didn't exist in 1992. In negotiations with the international community is where the map comes from, not the map that we're talking about. If you look, you will see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let's come to 1995, May, about this entry. Do you have any observation on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see here that there is a misunderstanding between Mr. Milosevic and myself and Mr. Karadzic and where he's using quite inappropriate language. This was at the time when the Contact Group plan was on the agenda. As for Orasje, I am not ruling out the possibility that at that time in 1995, when all the values were turned upside down, where force was on the agenda, where some of our territories were taken, the primary thing was for the army in Orasje not to have enemies behind their back in a very narrow corridor. I'm not ruling out that this was something that we discussed, but that was definitely never our policy right from the beginning to the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn quickly to page -- to 65 ter 25522 at page 25645.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's part of the discussion that you and Judge Orie were having about this video and about your assertion that there's a smaller area not yet held by our forces, it's not yet liberated yet, that is Orasje. And you say: "I think the map was a 1993 map or whenever. Perhaps it was 1992. Not quite sure ..." That was your testimony in the context of the very discussion about this map with Judge Orie that I raised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. 25645, lines 6 through 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, sir, even if I had said that, I kindly ask you to look at the map. There is no Srebrenica or Zepa on the map, so that means that it could not date from 1992, 1993, or 1994, but only from 1995 and not even that. The map is a proposal to the international community how to create a tripartite Bosnia and Herzegovina. If you look at it, you will see that it could not have been a map from 1992 or 1993 or 1994. Even if I had said that, I made a mistake. I was talking about the map that we had presented to the international community, I know that precisely, as a proposal. Of course the line of separation is there also, our front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I tender the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the next page as well. We'll admit these two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll add it to Exhibit P6516.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, your explanation that that map must be 1995 because it doesn't show Srebrenica, Zepa, or Gorazde, how does that make sense? Did you have Gorazde in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I said the map cannot date from 1992, 1993, or 1994. It can date from 1995. I'm saying that the map that I was talking about is the map indicating the line that was held by our forces, marking our front line. It could not have been the actual, real map from 1992 because none of the enclaves are there that existed at the time. So the map could not be from 1992, 1993, or 1994. It could possibly be from 1995, but this is a map that we put forward as a proposal to the international community. It's two maps, one is like a transparent film on top of it, the actual map, and then the lines of division that are on the transparency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I see, that was your proposal to the international community, that that horseshoe represented the portions of Bosnia and Herzegovina that you considered was Serbian and that you considered the international community should bestow on the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map was a proposal at one of the conferences. There are a number of press conferences where the same map appears. In Belgrade, Mr. Karadzic also interpreted this map as our proposal to be discussed at one of the conferences. As to whether it's a realistic one or not, that's a different matter, but it's a map dating from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. So two mistakes in this broadcast, number one, the reference to Orasje -- or in your testimony, number one, the reference to Orasje; and number two, the reference to the fact that this map dates from 1992 and 1993. Any other mistakes in your testimony to Judge Orie regarding this broadcast that you need to bring to our attention?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put five questions at the same time. I was clear. That map that I was explaining was a map that we gave to the international community, it was our proposal. Secondly, when I explained that, I said: Look, we are not holding all the territories that we -- that belong to us except for Orasje. I did mention the strategic goal -- well, I don't know if there were any other mistakes or errors. If you ask me, then I will be able to tell you. But I was never for capturing the territory of the other -- of another ethnic community that could not belong to us when the final division is decided on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, Mr. Krajisnik, you may -- you and your forces may not have been able to take Orasje during the course of the conflict, but as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Do we not have the date of that broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, it had to be contextually dated, Mr. President. It was dated by a witness or two, but before Mr. Krajisnik testified; and then it was dated by him. But the date does not appear on the broadcast itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the date appearing on the English translation as 1992 is not a correct one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's not a reflection of the specified date on the broadcast itself, no. But it was a reflection of the aggregation of testimony in the previous case and aggregation of testimony largely in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I might also add, and I'll check on that, it was part of materials that we received and -- so I also imagine that when it was originally dated in that manner it was related to the other portions of the broadcast that were provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the year does not appear in the B/C/S version, I just note that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I said, Mr. Krajisnik, your forces may not have been able to take Orasje, but as we know from the evidence in this case and as we can see from this horseshoe map and from what you stated, that there were many other places that were populated primarily by non-Serbs which were taken. For example, if we look at the right side of that horseshoe, among the municipalities included there is Foca, which you'll agree was a predominantly Muslim -- was a Muslim-majority municipality prior to the conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Foca was divided at the beginning of the war. If you want to say who the majority was, well there was almost an equal number of Serbs and Muslims. In the elections even a Serbian deputy from that municipality won. So the number of Muslims was practically equal to that of the Serbs, perhaps a percentage or two larger, but then part of the municipality was allocated to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we've received evidence in this case, including through statements made by Petko Cancar at the Assembly in front of you, that by -- that not that long after the conflict began that Foca had become almost an entirely Serbian municipality; that is, I think as Cancar said, you'd have trouble finding any Muslims within the territory of Foca which was geographically among the largest municipalities in Bosnia. I'd like to look at what you said when you went to Foca after the conflict began and after the municipality no longer had -- not only no longer had a Muslim majority, but had few Muslims at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's P06204. I'd like to play that. And the date of this broadcast is 21 May 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Brothers and sisters, high priests, president of Srbinje Municipal Assembly, members of the Assembly, dear Professor Kilibarda, dear people of Srbinje, it is a great pleasure to be among you after two and a half years. Today you are not as you were before. Now I see a true Serbian town, and you proudly bear your true Serbian name. You are the example to every Serb because all that was coming from this town you've managed to eliminate. You've prevented it from happening. From this town, from this community, the hardest things were aimed at the Serbian people by the then-leaders of the Serbian-Muslim organisation, the SDA. Then, Mr. Izetbegovic ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The video stopped. I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think this is enough for what you would like to ask me, so I don't think there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Was that you preparing the people of Foca for the return of the Muslim population after the conflict ended?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a barbed and spiteful question a little bit, Mr. Prosecutor, because I was giving a political speech here and I can explain every single thing. Of course today I would speak differently, but then it was war and I tried to choose carefully every word; and I can interpret each of those words, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We have that in evidence. I want to move on to what you said about the document known as Variant A and B, that is, the instructions of December 19th, 1991. Now, here in this trial you said in response to questions about -- from Dr. Karadzic that everything you say now is -- was also reflected in what you testified to in your own trial. And this appears here at 43201. You minimise the importance of the document. You said you didn't know when it was distributed and that was essentially it. What you said in your own case, and I'll ask you to confirm, is also that you don't remember the document being distributed, you didn't get the document at the time, if you had received that document you would have just put it away because you never found it was important, you never heard from any locality that they had implemented it, and you discussed how groundless and unnecessary it was; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all correct, except for this part that I had never heard of it. Perhaps that's an omission. I'm sure I did hear of it, but today I did feel that it was superfluous. Perhaps as far as the municipalities are concerned, the concern is there and I think it was not implemented in a number of municipalities, at least 50 or 60 per cent of them, and I think there could have been a recommendation for each municipality without the document A and B. The document A and B is quite illogical and difficult to implement had anyone wished to implement it. As for me not knowing when it was distributed, that is correct. I do not have any recollection on anybody distributing it in my presence. I really was not aware of anybody distributing the A and B document in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in connection with the Variant A and B document, Dr. Karadzic asked you at transcript page 43207 the following leading question: "Two days before that, on the 19th of December, did you attend the plenary session of the Serbian Democratic Party?" And you said: "I believe so. "Q. You've already discussed this. Was there any debate about papers A and B, debate and decision? "A. No." Then -- now, the fact is that the plenary that took place before the Assembly session on the 21st of December didn't take place on the 19th, it took place on the 20th. And let me show you two documents to indicate that. First, if we could look at P5792, an intercepted telephone conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Novakovic on the 19th of December. Here on the first page we see Dr. Karadzic talking to Novakovic and saying about some others: "They can go fuck themselves. I'll introduce ... this Friday I'll introduce a second-degree state of emergency and I'll teach everyone who fucks around a fuckin' lesson." Novakovic says: "Is that so?" Karadzic: "Yes, yes ... they were here from ... this region and they'll let you know about who needs to come. It's our Assembly session here on Saturday." So Saturday was the 21st, Friday was the 20th, and that was the date on which the plenary was held. And, secondly, I would like you to look at a portion of the Grkovic diary --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, excuse me. Can we finish this first. This piling up of documents is improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, does that refresh your recollection now in contrast to your response to Dr. Karadzic's leading question that the plenary was held on the 20th and not the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Karadzic was wrong. The plenary was not on the 20th, but the Deputies Club was held together with representatives or deputies from the SDS. We had a meeting with representatives of the SDS, deputies from the board. And so I probably wasn't present when this was distributed because I was doing this other thing. So when the -- this was being distributed, it's possible that I was in another office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to confirm that recollection, if we could look at 65 ter 08201 at English pages 58 through 59 and B/C/S 64. Just showing you the entry for the 19th, to orient, use the diary. If we could -- so we see here the entries for the 19th -- we show -- yeah, thank you. And then if we could turn to the next page, the 20th. And there we see the listing for the meeting of the Main Board and the Deputies Club, so the SDS representatives and the deputies as you referred to earlier. So again, that's a reflection of the fact that the large meeting which preceded the Assembly session, that is, the 4th Assembly Session on the 21st, took place on the 20th and not the 19th, as Dr. Karadzic suggested to you in his question during your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you're right. On the 20th, it had been scheduled for the 19th, as you saw on that paper a moment ago, at 12.00 at that, but it was held on the 20th. I think that you're right. I think it was on the 20th just before the session of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender that portion of the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whose diary is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is Mr. Grkovic, his diary. This was -- a portion of this was tendered by Dr. Karadzic earlier and during the -- when he tendered that, he mentioned that Mr. Grkovic was "my chef de cabinet in the Serbian Democratic Party." So this is the diary of Mr. Karadzic's chef de cabinet at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we include page 2 of this document? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think it would be appropriate to admit this entire document, 08201. This -- we've admitted Dr. Karadzic's agenda for 1995. It's been useful. It's been referred to different times. I think it would be useful also to have this admitted in its entirety for the same reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have any objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6520, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, the reason I asked for this date to be clarified is that there was a -- there's a telephone conversation between Dr. Karadzic and yourself that's in evidence, that's P2550, which refers to what happened at the previous day. So it was important to know what happened that previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIGER
utterances.text: And if we could call up P2550 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Tieger. Part of that diary was admitted already as evidence in our case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That would be D215 and it's discussed -- its admission or tendering was discussed at transcript pages 2713 through 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then why don't we admit it in its entirety as D215 instead of producing --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- another exhibit number. Yes, we'll strike out the P number, 6520.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Although I suspect for clarity there will have to be some -- I imagine the Registry can take care of that, some way to identify where in the diary the portion that was being discussed and tendered at 215 can be found so that there is no confusion about that, but that shouldn't be very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Registry will make sure to leave some reference to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. P2550, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A conversation between you, Mr. Karadzic -- Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 3, we see that there is a discussion about -- or a reference to Mr. Cizmovic. And Dr. Karadzic says: "You know what, who will implement what we issued last night?" And you say: "This Council of Ministers." He says: "But they can't run from municipality to municipality." You say: "Huh?" And he says: "They cannot run from municipality to municipality and say, Do this, do that or that." You say: "He won't run either." And Dr. Karadzic says: "But he must run." Now, that reference of Cizmovic running from municipality to municipality and implementing what we issued last night is a reference to the Variant A and B document and to Cizmovic's role in attempting to ensure that the municipalities move forward on its implementation; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not it. You can find an answer here in the next paragraph, if you take a look at that. You see where you read this and then later on it says: "Yes, but do you see what he is doing? But all right. It is not important. Well, you know, we put it in, you know, like an article. Then we down sized it, right." Mr. Cizmovic became chairman of the Council of Ministers and he was supposed to synchronise the members of the council that were supposed to pursue policy -- no, not policy, many decisions that were reached by the Assembly. So this is an answer -- this comment of mine is an answer to your question about Mr. Cizmovic as a member of the ministerial council who was supposed synchronise the implementation of the decisions on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Cizmovic, as you stated in your testimony in the Krajisnik -- in your own case was a "confidant" of Mr. Karadzic and "he kept him informed"; right? That's what you testified to in your case?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was a bit nasty there because Cizmovic is a Montenegrin like Mr. Karadzic, so perhaps I made a bit of a joke in terms of the confidence involved. He had no particular importance. Maybe he did inform Karadzic about certain things, but I would not say that he was a man of particular confidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender 25053, Mr. President, where those references are made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also testified --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we looked at the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. We can call it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, I have difficulty admitting the page we didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 65 ter 25522, lines 20 through 21 at page 25053.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before we move to that transcript, do you agree the -- it is the Variant A and -- document that you were talking about with Mr. Karadzic and you in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 65 ter 25522 I think is being called up. And the page as mentioned is 25053, lines 20 through 21. Can we scroll up, please. Well, it seems to be miscited here. One moment. Well, I'll return to that in a moment. Sorry, it's missed by one page, 25054 and the lines are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Mr. Cizmovic was a Montenegrin and so was Mr. Karadzic, and he was a confidant of Mr. Karadzic and he kept him informed ..." That was your testimony in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the continuation is very important and I explain why. It was this sort of nasty observation of mine, not really malicious or anything like that. I was alluding to the fact that most of them were Montenegrin. It's not that Cizmovic was that important. You will see from all these documents that he had no role, no particular role. He was co-ordinator of the Council of Ministers at first, or something like that as far as I can remember, but afterwards he was simply lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in keeping with that theme, you also stated in your testimony - and we'll be able to see the extent to which Mr. Cizmovic kept Mr. Karadzic informed - but you also said there were hundreds of representatives of Mr. Karadzic like that, meaning like Mr. Cizmovic, whom he sent into the field. And that's at 25070, lines 4 through 8. That was also your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of poor communication, because of different kinds of misinformation, because of different kinds of fear in terms of what was going on in the field, Mr. Karadzic kept trying to receive the right kind of information so that he could take certain measures, and that could be seen from his different statements when he alluded to certain information that he was receiving from the ground. And one of them was Mr. Cizmovic. It wasn't a countless number, but it was a large number of people who were similar to Cizmovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And the way you phrased it in 2006 is: "There were hundreds of representatives of Mr. Karadzic like that whom he sent into the field ..."; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right. I exaggerated a bit. It's not hundreds, but it was certainly a large number, a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I tender both those pages then, Mr. President, 25053 [sic] and 25070.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The second page that we are looking at, how do you know this is a reference to Cizmovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Because -- if you want to see the previous page to contextualise it, I'm happy with that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we look at the previous page. Yes, we'll admit these -- we'll add these three pages to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I misspoke. I said 25053, when of course we identified it correctly as 25054.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. As long as we're on the subject of Mr. Cizmovic, can we turn next to P2551. This is a telephone conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Cizmovic in the same day as the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For you, Mr. Tieger. Do you agree that the topic Mr. Karadzic and Krajisnik talked about through that intercept was not related to Variant A and B document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course not, Mr. President. My -- my -- I -- I -- I put to this witness that it was exactly about Variant A and B, and I'm going to take him through a number of subsequent documents which will, in our submission, make that point completely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your case is that that -- what they issued last night was the Variant A and B document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's why I focused on the distinction between the 19th and the 20th, that what happened the previous day, on the 20 -- the -- was -- the plenary session where this was distributed was the 20th rather than the 19th, as the leading question seemed to indicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I would like the witness to expand on the reason why he said: Absolutely no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I read this sentence where I said we appointed Cizmovic -- we brought him to a low level, we determined what his authority would be. Read that sentence. Cizmovic was chosen to be co-ordinator of the Council of Ministers, to co-ordinate their work from the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the decisions that would be made by the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina were supposed to be carried out by the Council of Ministers, and Mr. Cizmovic was supposed to co-ordinate that. Mr. Tieger can call up hundreds of pieces of evidence, but I'm saying that that document was not discussed in my presence at that plenary or at the Assembly. Maybe it was distributed but it wasn't discussed. The topic was completely different. It had to do with the work of the Council of Ministers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we upload the intercept, P2550, I remember it was page 3. Could you -- so Mr. Karadzic is saying: "You know what, who will implement what we issued last night? This Council of Ministers ..." So what was it what they issued last night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, different decisions, different requests. This, on the 21st -- the Assembly was held on the 21st and the Deputies Club, the Deputies Club was on the 20th, together with the representatives where we discussed different ideas, different decisions, a lot of that. And then on the following day, the Assembly, and that's where it was carried through. I'm saying here the Council of Ministers is supposed to implement these decisions, and after that I say that Cizmovic got this duty and you will find in documents that he was co-ordinator of the Council of Ministers. We are not mentioning Variants A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We're -- I don't know if 255 -- get back to 2551, conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Cizmovic, the same date as the intercept we looked at just now. If we could turn to English page 2 and move on to 3 as we discuss it, and B/C/S page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic tells Cizmovic: "The most important thing now in this very moment is that those papers those ..." And Cizmovic interjects: "To the realisation." Karadzic: "Right, right." Cizmovic: "Fine." Karadzic: "That is the most important." Cizmovic again interjects: "The most important would be if ..." And Karadzic says: "You have a full authorisation to visit all our municipalities, including even those where there is no ... and all those there who are ours." Now, on that same date, this is Cizmovic and Karadzic talking, and those papers that Karadzic is talking about is a reference to Variant A and B which had been recently distributed and needed to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a thankless job for me to try to interpret Mr. Karadzic, but I'll try, although that is not proper. In the Serbian language it says: The most important thing at this moment is those papers. If he meant A and B, he would have said: That paper. But there were several decisions, suggestions, here. A lot of things had to be implemented. Just take the agenda of the Assembly on the 21st of November, and that was the previous day, the Deputies Club. Really, when Mr. Karadzic testifies, he can explain this to you, but this is how I interpret it. I don't know, they could have agreed on papers A and B, but I know that this A and B paper in my presence was not officially discussed at this Deputies Club. Maybe it was distributed, probably it was distributed, because I see that many witnesses said that it was distributed. I was not present and I don't know how that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at 2596, a telephone conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Miroslav on the 7th of January, 1992. If we could turn to English page 7, B/C/S page 8. Dr. Karadzic says in response to Miroslav saying: "This is not a time for science, right?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC SAYS
utterances.text: "No, it's not a time for science. It is time to take over real functions, real functions ... this, this and this real function and chop-chop ... and there isn't any ... in the sense of that paper ... I don't know ... that paper of ours ... level one - level two." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, that discussion is another reflection of Dr. Karadzic's continuing focus on the need to implement Variant A and B on the ground, that is, the document referring to level one and level two; right? That was a big part of his focus at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should ask Mr. Karadzic about that. I assure you, and I would like to point out, in my presence Variant A and B was not discussed, we did not take any positions regarding that, and whatever people said they could have spoken about that, but A and B Variant was not carried through. Perhaps in 10 or 20 municipalities out of a hundred or 50 or whatever the number was, however many there were. Mr. Karadzic can explain this to you. Maybe he did speak about Variants A and B, level one, level two, but this document did not constitute any kind of important document. It was not any kind of evidence in terms of our pursuit of policy. It was unnecessary, if you want my view. Not unnecessary from the point of view of fear. People had the right to express their fear, but as far as the functioning of the municipalities is concerned, it was completely unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P2552, English page 7, B/C/S page 8, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Telephone conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Cizmovic on the 16th of January, 1992. Here discussing, as we see from the earlier part of the intercept, what's been going on -- what results Cizmovic is achieving in the field. As we see, he discusses with Dr. Karadzic: "I've talked to Bijeljina, they're prepared for full co-operation, it's the same case with northern Bosnia." And then he says at the bottom of page 1 -- page 7 of the English: "To what extent are they prepared to implement the first level of the instructions? What are the problems? What do they need help with? So that I am even prepared to form a sort of team with your help ..." So this is a reflection of what Cizmovic was running from municipality to municipality to implement, that is, the first level of the instructions. It's crystal clear from this intercept, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. This is an example for you. Bijeljina, what was Mr. Cizmovic looking for over there? Serbs are an absolute authority. They do not need Variants A or B. Why would they establish a municipality? They have 100 per cent authority there. He went there to implement other decisions, I think, of the Council of Ministers. Or the man may have had some other reason. Perhaps he misunderstood his role. In Bijeljina he had no reason to go there to carry out Variants A and B because it was 100 per cent Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know of any other document containing instructions divided in different levels or reference to -- or even non-written instructions to -- that were split up on different levels? You don't, do you? Variant A and B is the only one in existence at that time. And that's exactly what you told Judge Orie when he asked you that same question.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not disputing the existence of Variants A and B as documents. Large number of witnesses confirmed that it had been distributed and I believe them. All I'm saying is that this document is completely insignificant. Even if it was implemented, it was implemented only partially. There may have been two or three parallel activities. One of them was maybe a peripheral one, including Variants A and B, and the rest were essential Assembly decisions that had to be implemented. So Mr. Cizmovic maybe made a confusion there and I'm telling you that Variants A and B were irrelevant for what you're interested. It may have been relevant with regard to fear, and the soldiers rightfully pointed that out in view of the experience from World War II, and I only learned about this paper during my trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break for half an hour. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce Lili Dobreva from Bulgaria, who's working as a legal intern for our Defence team. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to look at a few documents in connection with your testimony to this Court that Variant A and B was irrelevant, that's at 33, 7, that you only learned about it at your trial, also on page 33 of our discussion today, and that it was never discussed in your presence, that's at page 31. So I'd like to turn first to the Assembly session -- the 6th Assembly Session held on the 25th and the 26th of January, and that's at - let me just find the reference - P1349, English page 12 and B/C/S page 25. Now, as we're waiting for that to come up, Mr. Krajisnik, recalling the date of this session, the 26th of January, 1992, can you confirm your testimony in your case that this was a special and extraordinary session called to consider what should be done in the face of what you term the unconstitutional decisions by the Bosnian Assembly on the referendum of independence which had occurred the previous day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was an extraordinary session related to the BH Assembly session that was to be held.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the topic of discussion at that Assembly, what people were talking about as you acknowledged during your own testimony, was what to do in response to that; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the main task was to persuade the deputies to attend the joint session of BH Assembly where the referendum was to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the deputies were talking about other things; for example, Mr. Vjestica at page 12 of the English and page 25 of the B/C/S talked about "setting up our own state" and the immense duties they faced in that regard and how there must be a great deal of hard work and discipline and that an operative plan should be drawn up to define tasks and dead-lines. If we could turn back, you can see -- the next previous page you can see who the speaker is. Okay, so you can see Mr. Vjestica talking, and he begins by saying this is a time where protracted speeches -- not a time for protracted speeches and a time to move forward. If we turn to the next page. Next page, please. We can see him talking about setting up dead-lines, the need for discipline, and the need to execute operative plan and so on. And as you acknowledged in your own testimony, the discussion about what to do in response became pretty concrete pretty early; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about later, but what Mr. Vjestica is saying here is clear to me. He is underlying that we are constantly and unsuccessfully trying to reach a democratic agreement with the other side. He expressed his concern about the situation in his area where there were lots of Muslim soldiers and paramilitary forces that had been established in Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "The operative plan should also be drawn up to define tasks precisely, those charged with executing them and the dead-lines for their completion." He did say that at the 6th Session; right? You can see it right there. And then Mr. Cizmovic spoke shortly thereafter, that's at page 14 of the English, and e-court page 29 in the B/C/S. And in the context of this concrete discussion about the steps that should be taken in response to this unconstitutional decision, as you put it, Mr. Cizmovic said at this extraordinary session -- to solve the problem he proposed: " ... an urgent operationalisation and a declaration on the establishment and promulgation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Tasks set out in the instructions of 19 December 1991 should be carried out." Now, that is a clear reference to the Variant A and B document. In fact, it's a reference to the document in terms of its very title; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is making reference to the document of the 19th of December, probably Variants A and B. But, you see, he says here that a decision to declare the republic of the Serbian people, and on 9th of January we already did that. We proclaimed our own republic. So if you have your republic, then any discussion about Variants A and B becomes superfluous and irrelevant. I don't know what reason he had to make reference to this document. Perhaps you should ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So do I understand that you're now modifying your testimony to the Court a few moments ago, that this was never discussed in your presence; and now you want to say: Well, it was discussed in my presence but it's an irrelevant document, so why does it matter?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I totally did not accept that because I didn't see that as important. My concern was hard to persuade the deputies to attend the next day's session of the BH Assembly. That is why it was irrelevant to me. I didn't pay attention which date he mentioned, 19th of December or any date in 2005 or whatever. What I'm saying that there was no discussion. He may have mentioned it, as he probably did, but you can see that nobody continued with the discussion about this. It was only Mr. Cizmovic who mentioned this specific date, although this date could be quite meaningless, it didn't mean anything to me; therefore, it escaped my memory. And you can see further on in the minutes that there was no further efforts to the 19th of December. I suppose so, maybe somebody else did, though, but I don't know. So this document was totally not on the agenda of the Assembly of the Serbian People. Somebody may have mentioned it, I'm not ruling out that possibility though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, why don't we turn to the very next time this group got together, which is the 14th February extended Session of the Main Executive Boards and Deputies Club which is P00012.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Karadzic mentioned level two, but this didn't mean anything either. It may have been some instruction or whatever, but that was not discussed by the Serbian Assembly nor was it implemented in the way that you are trying to portray. And I know what you are trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, what I'm trying to do is present in the course of this examination the contemporaneous documents reflecting exactly what was discussed and how it was discussed. You say here: "I know that Mr. Karadzic mentioned level two ..." Well, the fact of the matter is Mr. Karadzic referred to the Variant A and B document four times in the course of his presentation and concluded with the fact that that's why we called you here today, to intensify, to introduce "the second level and to intensify the functioning of the government at any cost and every single millimetre of our territory." So it wasn't simply mentioning it, it was emphasising it and moving it up from level one to level two; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tieger. I didn't say that I knew that he spoke about this. I don't remember. I do know that this was presented as evidence in my trial and we commented on it as well as other witnesses did, and I can assert that as official authorities nor did the Serbian Assembly take any position on that. It was only a document produced by people who were concerned and that was implemented somewhere. I don't know what kind of document that was, whether it was complete or not. Why somebody's trying to portray this document as something that was the product of a conspiracy. Can you please find me any Municipal Assembly or five Municipal Assemblies that have implemented what is contained in Variants A and B. I assure you that not even the municipalities with absolute Muslim majority did not -- did implement that. You heard that the Crisis Staff came into being two years later. Variants A and B were not implemented as they did -- it was not a secret document. It did not bear any relevance. It was totally immaterial.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to a couple of other documents, but let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not recorded in the transcript that Mr. Krajisnik said that the document was benign, unharmful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If somebody gave it to me today I would say: All right. I would read it and I wouldn't see any -- anything bad about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that you said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I confirm that, that it was a benign document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also -- I'm going to go to the issue of what Municipal Assemblies did or didn't do, also in the context of your claim that no one discussed it in your presence. But I also noted in your testimony earlier you said you would have known about municipal Crisis Staffs if there were any, but you didn't.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did I misunderstand you when you said earlier that you didn't know about the establishment of municipal Crisis Staffs in the period of time before the conflict, that is, between December 19 and April 1992? Or did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I knew that Crisis Staffs existed, but that was not - how shall I put it? - a planned action. It might have occurred spontaneously. I was working in a company and if the workers rebel they immediately set up a Crisis Staff. Crisis Staff were not a customary way to do things in the former system. I know that there were Crisis Staffs when barricades were erected. I knew about the Crisis Staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm talking about municipal Crisis Staffs, not Crisis Staffs in random companies. Didn't you say to this Court you would have known about municipal Crisis Staffs if there were any, but you didn't? And now you're saying you did know about Crisis Staffs. Did you know about municipal Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, do not put words into my mouth. I said that I knew about the Crisis Staff relating to the barricades and at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I said it was possible that Crisis Staffs did exist - I don't remember - but that was not a plan. There was no agreement to do that. It happened spontaneously. There was no directive issued by the SDS to set up Crisis Staffs. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 21, page 39, it was erroneously written "Crisis Staffs were not a customary way," whereas it should be "were a non-customary way." The witness said, "They were not a non-customary way of solving problems."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have to say that is one of the least helpful clarifications I've ever heard. Maybe the witness better be asked. I'm not sure what Dr. Karadzic is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm -- I understood that -- it's better to ask the witness. Do you remember the question -- do you follow the issue? What was it that you said? Could you repeat what you said, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The setting up of Crisis Staffs in the former system was not an unusual way to operate, so it was quite normal to set them up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Crisis Staffs were not a non-customary way to do things. Yes. So you agree with Mr. Karadzic's intervention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn to P01403, page 347 in the English, page 304 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document, Mr. Tieger and Mr. Robinson, when I discussed the rescheduling of the sitting in the week of 9th of December, I didn't realise that there's no courtroom available on Friday, 13th of December, due to the Appeals Chamber's hearing as well as Mladic hearing. So we'll go back to the original sitting plan, Monday to Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Good fortune for Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in any event, I thank the parties for their co-operation. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Here's what Dr. Karadzic said looking back on what happened in 1991 and 1992: [As read] "Please remember how we used to work before the war. Everything was as clear as day in the municipalities where we were majority and in those where we were minority. Do you remember the Instruction A and Instruction B? We had Crisis Staffs and it was clear that they were the authority. They could make mistakes but they were still the authority. The people were not left without the authority because there was a Crisis Staff." So when Dr. Karadzic was calling upon everybody in the Assembly to remember how it was in 1991 and 1992, were you the only person in the room who didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're really trying to insult me and that's not fair, but I will give you an answer. It is possible that Karadzic said that, but quite simply when somebody was delivering a speech I'm not paying attention to some information that at that point I thought were irrelevant and maybe I wasn't listening carefully. I suppose that this is what he said, and if Mr. Karadzic knew that the A and B Variant documents were distributed, he probably mentioned that. But I assure you that I never saw in practice whether it was distributed or implemented. That's what I said. I never disputed that someone may have received this document. The point is that this document did not produce any significant effects, definitely not. We're not talking about whether a municipality did receive it. It might have received it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am trying to find where this refers to the year 1991 in this text, and I can't do -- find it. So could Mr. Tieger please say specifically whether he's speaking about the period before April 1992 or after April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think Mr. Tieger was quoting from this document when he referred to 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to P975 very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asking about what the municipalities did or didn't do, posing the rhetorical question: Show me a municipality that acted on this. So here at P975, we see that Ilidza formed the Serbian Municipal Assembly "in accordance with the given instructions of the Serbian Democratic Party of BiH Main Board ...," and it provides the specific number, 079 "of 19 December 1991 ..." And if we can scroll down and then turn to the next page, please. This document was signed and it was forwarded personally to you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One more document, Mr. Krajisnik. If we could turn to P1377, English page 148 and B/C/S page 127 through 28, another document bearing on your claim that Variant A and B was irrelevant, that you only learned about it during your trial, and that it was never discussed in your presence. This is a session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, the 33rd Session in 1993, and here we see the president of the Jajce municipality speaking. And here's what he relates. First he notes: "If we go back a little and recall the material which came from the Main Board for work in the field, there was Variant A and B. Variant A was for municipalities where the Serbs were a majority, Variant B for municipalities in which they were not, like Jajce ... then, pursuant to those guide-lines we formed a Municipal Assembly and later formed municipal organs of government. All that was done before the war ... on the 27th of January 1992 ...," and he explains some of the things they did. So, first of all, that's a reflection of the discussion in front of you and the other representatives about the existence and implementation of Variant A and B, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no deputy in the municipality of Jajce or Ilidza. There was no Council of Citizens, and perhaps people did act pursuant to the document they received at that time. But when a discussion is being held, I wasn't really paying attention whether somebody mentioned some documents or not or if something could be linked with something else that would be important for me to answer right now. You see --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krajisnik please repeat what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You are speaking too fast, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Forgive me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have to repeat from where you said you were not really paying attention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that in the municipality of Jajce there was no deputy from that place in the Assembly, and perhaps they, pursuant according to Variant A and B that they received at the time which -- when the plenary together with the Deputies Club was in operation. I also mentioned the previous document. I said this decision about forming the municipality of Ilidza, perhaps it reached the secretary. It wasn't given to me. He registered it. Important to me was that the decision was made, if it was important, and problem solved. And now, had I known that I would have to reply about that here, I would have read each decision and then there would be a decision A and B. I would say: What is that? And then I would make an inquiry. I mean, it wouldn't have occurred to me then or today. It could have been formed by one or the other SDS president pursuant to a recommendation of the Assembly without any problems at all, without any Variant A and B. He had the Assembly document on the formation and he could have sent it to me. Why would he need Variant A and B?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it's your testimony to this Trial Chamber, Mr. Krajisnik, that you weren't paying attention when the president of Jajce municipality said: [As read] "When according to instructions we were to form the Serbian municipality of Jajce on the orders of Dr. Karadzic and yourself, I conducted talks with all the Assemblymen in the joint Assembly who were Serbs and a single one agreed to join the joint, i.e., the Serbian municipality of the Serbian municipality of Jajce ... all the others refused. As we had no one to augment, the presidents of the local boards became members ex-officio. At a gathering in Sarajevo, I asked Dr. Karadzic and you what I should do in that event and we agreed that the presidents of the local boards should join by virtue of their office, as had been agreed ..." So when the president of Jajce municipality outlined the background of the Variant A and B document, talked about the implementation that they were able to achieve, identified their attempt to further implement it and the obstacles they encountered based on the orders of you and Dr. Karadzic as he said explicitly, and then related and recalled how he went to you and Dr. Karadzic for counselling, you weren't paying any attention to this?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have talked to me. I don't recall that now. He probably did talk to me. I have no reason as president of the Assembly to tell him: Take Variant A and B, when he has the recommendation. Here's the recommendation, take it from the Assembly if you need to do that. Why would I need once we adopted the recommendation, why would we take Variant A and B before the Assembly? We could have done that, adopted it before the Assembly. But the recommendations were adopted before the Variant A and B, so the president of the Jajce municipality could have received an answer from me: Here's the recommendation, take it and constitute. Only pursuant to the -- only the recommendation is relevant in the formation. The A and B Variant is not relevant. It's an instruction, it's an expression of concern, but the only valid document was the recommendation. This other was not something that was adopted by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to a different topic. At transcript page 43340 of your testimony here in your examination-in-chief, you describe the taking of UN personnel as hostages as "a desperate attempt on the part of our army to prevent further air-strikes." So once again, you point to the army as being responsible for actions and not the political leadership. But the fact of the matter, Mr. Krajisnik, is that the political leadership, as always, was behind this, and in that regard I'd like to look at P5607. This is a transcript of an intercepted telephone conversation of the 30th of May, 1995, involving Todor Dutina, yourself, and Dr. Karadzic. And if we turn to the third page, first you can -- well, maybe first I'll take you through it quickly. You see Dutina talking to Milenko Karisik, another early participant. You are put on the phone at the top of page 3 in the English. Dutina asks you: "Let me tell you, Momo, that things aren't bad at all. Just take care. Is Radovan somewhere near?" You say: "He isn't. He's there." Then a few lines later you say: "Wait until I switch a call to Karadzic so we all can hear. Is that fine?" Karadzic comes on the phone on page 5. You say to him: "Radovan, here is Todor; speak up Todor; now Radovan is also listening ..." Dutina expresses some concerns about confusion that may result from an issue related to the involvement of a French intermediary. Dutina says: "Nobody should ... let me tell you, Radovan, we made a move and now we should wait for a move of the other side." Karadzic says: "Fine, their move was to send a negotiator that left empty-handed." And Dutina says, as we turn the page in the English: "That's the way it should be." And then you say: "And please, what did Jovanovic say?" Seeking clarification, Dutina says: "That an intermediary from France is being expected, et cetera." That was the issue that Dutina expressed some concern about. Karadzic says: "Intermediary in what? In the release of the hostages?" Dutina says: "They are not interested in anything else, you have to know that." Karadzic says: "We are not interested in letting them go as much as they are interested in us letting them go." Dutina: "Let me tell you, they should be kept until final solution." Karadzic: "That's our decision, that's out of the question, there is no release." And Dutina goes on to say well, people are a bit confused. Karadzic explains that the contact was irrelevant --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we have Serbian page displayed relevant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Karadzic explains that that was irrelevant. Dutina tries to say: "Look, they know what you eat." And you say: "Don't frighten us. It's not true that they know." Dutina says: "I'm not frightening you." And you say: "Well, they just pretend to know." And then you say: "If they did know, then why didn't they know that we would do this?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page for English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's on page 7 of the English, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krajisnik, this wasn't about some desperate action by the army.
