This is about an event that was planned and implemented -- planned by and implemented at the behest of the political leadership, as we've seen in other instances. And that's exactly what's being referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you were reading the intercept from here and there, so I couldn't put together all of the parts, but I will try to comment. Mr. Todor Dutina, whom I recall -- who I recall was absent at the time and by nature he's a man prone to panic. And he called us to talk to us and you saw how he said that foreigners knew what we were having for lunch, so this was exaggeration and that was the tone of the conversation. I repeat now that I don't know all the particulars precisely, but they can be found in the evidence here. For us, for me, the arrest of those soldiers -- actually, detaining the soldiers and showing that publicly on television was a desperate attempt to prevent further bombing, and what it says here, they could have known, the military and the political leadership warned several times in relation to their threats that they would bomb us, that they would consider that to be as NATO's interference as one of the sides in the conflict. I believe, I'm not sure now, that the initiative and the whole implementation was carried out by the army. Perhaps this can be seen from the evidence. If there's any evidence or an order by Mr. Karadzic, in that case I'll withdraw this assertion of mine. But my impression at the time was that this was a desperate attempt by the army, this is how the people understood it as well, in order to thwart bombing. Why would you want to do that publicly? Nobody wanted to harm those soldiers. You saw that when those three airmen were captured who had parachuted down, the local population accepted them as their very own. Our people don't have anything against the soldiers or the people, but they are against the policy that prompted those people to come and bomb us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it may have been the military that put their hands on the hostages and seized them and scattered them to various places around the territory of RS where they were placed, but it was the political leadership, you and Dr. Karadzic, who were full square behind that from the beginning, indeed even before it happened, as reflected in this intercept. This intercept reflects full backing for everything that's going on and reflects the fact that it was anticipated beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me the date of this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May 30th, 1995, as I mentioned at the outset.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 30th of May, 1995, is a period of major dissent or a split between the civilian authorities - I'm not going to talk about personal relationships - but it was personally a matter between Mladic and Karadzic. I don't believe that this was a -- had this been an initiative of Mr. Karadzic that Mr. Mladic would have implemented it. If this had been taken as a desperate attempt to thwart further bombing, we would not have taken this -- we would not -- we would have only done that on this pretext.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krajisnik please repeat what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, please speak slowly. No, just a second. You have to repeat from when you talked about desperate attempt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise deeply to the Trial Chamber and to others. Mr. Tieger inspires me to speak fast because a number of times I have told him that this was a desperate move, and that is how I understood it. And now I repeat, in 1995, May 1995, it's practically the end of the war and there was a split between the military and the civilian authorities. If there is any document indicating that Karadzic ordered the arrest of hostages, as you say, then that document could provide an answer to your question. All it could have said, if there was such an order - but I don't think there is, I'm not aware of it - he could have said: Let that be a matter of thwarting further bombings because we had warned several times as well as the army, both Mr. Karadzic and those who talked with representatives of the international community, if -- if NATO interferes with -- if it bombs our positions, then it will become a party to the conflict because it will place itself at the side of our enemies. I know that there was such warnings given, but I repeat: I understood this as a desperate move in order to prevent further bombing because the bombing was awful. There was a lot of panic, destruction of military, civilian, and communications facilities in Republika Srpska at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, throughout the process of the hostage-taking, you continued to express your endorsement for it, support for it, involvement in it, responsibility for it, and to stress your awareness of the great leverage that the hostages gave you, that is, that they were a kind of ace up your sleeve, and that you wouldn't be giving up that advantage easily. You wouldn't sell these hostages cheap. That was your position during this entire period of time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put five questions at the same time, but I will answer. Correct, but -- because I believed that this would be a way to prevent further bombardments. After a bombing like that -- my wife already also was a casualty, so I know what that means. But if you refer to my telephone conversations in 1992 -- not in 1995, excuse me, but bombing was conducted then so I know what it is. So if you referred to telephone conversations of mine with people abroad who spoke about hostages who were saying: You shouldn't release them, and so on and so forth. I talked with people then who were not informed about things so they could have said: You're crazy, you don't know what you're doing, you're advising us to do something inappropriate. I was trying to end a conversation that I disagreed with. I repeat: My support was towards preventing further bombing, that's how I understood it, because I saw that. I felt sorry for those men. I saw that on television, but they also showed the destruction throughout Republika Srpska. All I prayed for was for the bombing to stop, and that was my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. One point of clarification. You were trying to say there, it didn't come across clearly, that your earlier testimony and your brief reference here to your wife's death had nothing to do with the bombing in 1995, that that happened in 1992? I know you mentioned your wife's death twice now in the context of a discussion about the hostage-taking and the NATO bombing, but you were conflating two periods of time. Unfortunately, your wife died in 1992; correct? So I just want to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife was killed in 1992 and I said here I know what bombing means when bombs start falling, and bombs were dropping on Pale at that time. So there's an incredible amount of fear and it's a problem and you want that to stop immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at a couple of the intercepts that you alluded to in your answer. First if we can turn to 65 ter 328 -- 32 -- let's turn to P2271 first, please. So this is a conversation on the 3rd of June, 1995, between you and Mr. Vinkovic, who states at page 1: "Look here, as you predicted and as you said, the West would unite because they will be angry about what you've done." And you say: "I know." And then he goes on in his response to say: "However, now they are pointing their finger at who is to blame for such a situation. If you hold on for a while in this gambit, you'll see how they are disintegrating. That's why one begins to put pressure on families ...," et cetera. And he says: "I think that this played a great role because they have stated and are openly writing and saying that they cannot do anything" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please move it to the next page. I don't see that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that was in the bottom part of the page we were just looking at, Mr. Krajisnik, where Vinkovic begins "mej djutim." If we can turn back, I think that's where I was reading from. You see down there at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "I think that this played a great role because they have stated and are openly writing and saying that they cannot do anything to you as long as you're holding hostages. They can't make a single normal plan that they'll follow because every plan they want to follow implies the use of military force and they cannot do that because they'll endanger the lives of those hostages -- of these hostages. Therefore, the hostages are of vital importance to you regardless of what anyone else may be telling you." And you say: "My dear man, we let some go and we captured some others." Then if we continue on to the next page, that's toward the bottom of the page, same thing in English, please. Vinkovic says: "But look, hold on to the hostages. That's a fantastic card! Don't ever forget that Saddam got destroyed when he released the hostages." And you say: "Yes, yes. We're doing that. We have an excellent method. We always have an ace up our sleeve." And then Vinkovic says, and I think that continues on to the next page in your language: "The hostages are the cheapest anti-aircraft protection, better than a missile because they never miss." So that's one of the telephone conversations that you alluded to in your previous answer, Mr. Krajisnik; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be very good to continue with the text and then you would see that I replied to his assertions with a joke.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By saying: "We've got the support of the greatest power in the world"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please continue and then you will see exactly which power I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, I -- I am finished pointing out those portions of the intercept that I wanted to bring to your attention and to the Court's attention, but if you want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see. Let us see [overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. President. He is -- I'm sorry. But I'm happy to let Mr. Krajisnik do that, but he's asking me to pursue the intercept. I'm just turning it back to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, next page, please. Now, tell us what you wanted to say, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I deeply respect, value Mr. Tieger, but he's a specialist in reading an excerpt of the text and then he would like a response to something else that is also important -- without submitting something else that is also important. I said to my collocutor: We have the greatest power in the world. He said: Whom? And I said: You. And then I said: The diaspora that is supporting us. I wanted to bring the conversation to a more relaxed tone. I did not wish to disrespect the person at the other end of the line. So when you read it, you can see that, and this is important. If you would like a true response, you need to read the whole text. I don't remember the entire conversation. Actually, I'd never read it until I'd spent some time here in prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I'm following you. How is the issue of support from diaspora related to this hostages issue, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our entire conversation was a conversation with a person from the Serbian diaspora, and he kept giving this advice in terms of radical moves: Don't let them go, and so on and so forth. I did not agree with that, we are no power. And then in order to lighten things up, I said: We have the support of the greatest power in the world, God and you and the diaspora. And I wanted to say by that that what he was saying was not realistic. I did not want to offend him by saying: What are you telling us? What you're saying is nebulous. So anyway, this is one of the conversations I had with people from the diaspora.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 65 ter 32818, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a conversation between you and Petar Makara on June 2nd, 1995. Mr. Makara begins by expressing concern that the hostages will be handed over prematurely, which he considers a kind of treason. He states to you, this is in the second big block: "Your only hope and guarantee is that you will be able to keep the hostages. There is no way they will sacrifice so many people" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page are we on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's the first page, Mr. President, second block of the first page: "There is no way they will sacrifice so many people which you already hold."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He says that to Milena, your secretary, and then you get on the line, and on the second page he continues in the same vein. You say to him: "... we are not" -- this is the second block on this page, 2. "... we are not crazy to release them. Let them be scared, what intervention groups of theirs and others, those are stories for little children."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Should we --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you continue and you can read the entirety --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure we are on the correct page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we should go back a page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, and you'll see it here: "... we are not crazy to release them. Let them be scared, what intervention groups of theirs and others, those are stories for little children." You say: "We are unable to gather them. Here already for two days we are collecting them, and not that we could find them, that is all scattered." Makara wanted to convey and then tried a couple of times, he says: "To convey the message that it is very important, that you are already uniting with RSK ... and the Serbs are already mixed there with Knin, and so you could capture many of those from the West, which would be twice as important." If you continue on to the next page in B/C/S and English. After speaking briefly about Western Slavonia, you say: "Here, the two of us understand each other even when we are not talking openly. Please, tell my namesake, he has to make sure that all those goods have to be sold expensively. It is selling, don't be ..." And Makara says: "Let me tell you this, in the Falkland islands the British lost 255 men. They won't let themselves lose 255 men over Bosnia which isn't theirs." And you say: "Not because of Bosnia." He goes on to talk about the relations with America and how the politicians in the West only care about winning elections, rather than the number of people killed. And then after you speak saying you hope he understands you, he says: "I believe, exactly that I wanted to tell you, if you know," which at least as it's written, "a lot of hostages, the way the West has been working for the Muslims, they will shift and work for you." And you say: "Fine, we need those people. Believe me, we are very pleased, very pleased, because there are many things we have achieved and which we have mentioned ..." And then if we turn to the last page, please. You are concluding the conversation: "Please say hello to my namesake and please know that this is a great thing, although they are telling us that this is stupid. This is a great finished match, and now our partners who had to give in can fidget as much as they want, but they have to pay. This is a payment ..." And then Makara says -- goes on to talk about taking an enclave: "... any one, because any one you take would make a precedent and it is clear to the entire world that the UN is useless and that it is time to withdraw. There has been some talk about this already." And you say: "... we shall look into some of the plans, it is being worked on ...," and then you mention a small problem you can't discuss on the phone. Mr. Krajisnik, that's another reflection of your support, as you mentioned, for the retention of the hostages and another reflection of the conversations with people in the diaspora about the hostage-taking, conversations that you alluded to in your previous answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be a good thing if you were to go back to the previous telephone conversation where there is mention of Mr. Makara, and then you will see what this Novakovic thinks about Makara and then it will all be clear to you why this kind of conversation took place. He says that he's crazy, or words to that effect. You can go back to that other intercept and you'll see. He's a good man, but he's an idealist, and he has these "idee fixe." My answer is the same. When I talked to people from the diaspora, I didn't want to offend them, I tried as much as I could to speak in riddles in order to satisfy him, but not to openly agree with him. You see, over there Mr. Makara is an old man. He called very often. He was worried. He offered advice, of course unrealistic advice that we disagreed with. I repeat, the hostages were our trump card, if I can put it that way, and that's what it says here, in order to avert the danger of bombing our positions. The intention was not to kill people, but to prevent terrible things that were happening in our area then. So go back and see what this other Momcilo said about Makara.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6520, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 65 ter 32822, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this is a conversation roughly a couple of weeks later on June 15th, 1995, again between you and Makara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for reference, if you could remind us of the exhibit number where Makara was referred to, as indicated by Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P -- I believe Mr. Krajisnik was referring to P2271, which was the intercept that preceded this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't have to go back to that intercept at the moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With Mr. Novakovic, the telephone conversation with Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. If necessary, Mr. Karadzic will deal with it in his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, just so there's no confusion, P2271 is a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Vinkovic. The only conversation with Mr. Novakovic that I recall is the one that we -- between --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Momcilo I think it's Ninkovic, you're right. I know his first name is Momcilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. We're now at 65 ter 32822 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You didn't put that question, but it's evident that, Mr. Krajisnik, you agree that it was your conversation with Makara that we just admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We're at 65 ter 32822.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, this is a conversation on the 15th of June, 1995, between you and Makara. And it begins by him talking about an attack. You continue talking about -- you move on fairly quickly to the issue Mr. Makara had raised before, that's in the middle of the page: "We still think you made a mistake, letting those hostages go." You say: "Mr. Makara, let me tell you ... it was the biggest deal and quite a lucrative one. I am not saying we could have gotten more out of it, but it would have been useless having the UNPROFOR personnel and not having ..." And then I'll give you a moment to familiarise yourself with the rest of it. Again Makara emphasises that an enclave should be taken, just to make clear that UNPROFOR doesn't mean anything over there. And if we could turn to the end of the intercept. I will go slowly so you can see the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I need the previous page in English, please. Thanks. And you can go to the second page in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You can conclude the conversation by assuring him: "Believe me, this is the best deal. All the rest would ... these hostages would have simply spoiled if we had kept them without being able to sell them properly. We are very pleased." So, Mr. Krajisnik, that's another one of the conversations between you and people in the diaspora that you referred to in your previous answers; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the best example of him advocating a very radical view, that the hostages should be kept to the very end. Our army released the hostages -- they were not hostages, actually. They were soldiers that had been taken prisoner. And then, indeed, the Serb positions were bombed again and that's why we lost lots of territory. Makara is right here, although he's not a very bright man or a very wise one, he was right from his point of view. But politically, we could not have kept the hostages. I mean, I keep saying "hostages," and that's your terminology. We could not have kept these soldiers longer. The decision was made, Mr. Mladic agreed on that, he released the hostages, and I think that that was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would tender 65 ter 32822.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6521, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And again, you confirm that interlocutor here is -- one of the interlocutors was you, Mr. Krajisnik, in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as far as I can see, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You confirm that this conversation took place? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that conversation. There were many. I assume it is, but I cannot be sure that that is that conversation, that it's the same one. Maybe it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, at page 43325 you said during your examination-in-chief: "The army that was in Sarajevo very often, very often provoked our army. They would hit them in order to elicit a response, if I can put it that way. That was based on a political decision -- I mean the Muslim and Croat side, or rather, the Muslim side in this situation. They wanted to represent Sarajevo as a victim and to represent us, our army, as an aggressor, people who were attacking in order to take a territory." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you cast this as responses from the Serb army, but, in fact, these -- and so again you're focusing on the actions of the army rather than any actions of the political leadership. But it's true, is it not, that the political leadership also urged and co-ordinated retaliation against Muslim positions and the Muslim population in the form of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm asking a question. I don't need a --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I think Mr. Tieger is putting the Prosecution's case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just interested in this part, the population, where it was that we asked for the civilian population to be targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's too bad that Mr. Karadzic feels that -- now he feels that, again, Mr. Krajisnik can't answer my questions. Before he thought he couldn't answer his questions unless he was leading. It's a question, the witness can answer it, and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. But for clarity, why don't you put your question again, which was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The testimony you gave at 43325, Mr. Krajisnik, addresses responses - and that was in the context of discussions about the shelling of Sarajevo - responses by the army. So I'm asking you whether or not it isn't true that the political leadership got involved in the issue of responding or retaliating against the Muslims in the form of shelling?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there are two questions here, I'm going to answer both of them. The first question, at the time I had information to the effect that our army was responding to the provocations coming from the other side. Now, after having had a look at numerous documents from my case, I'm absolutely sure of that. At that time, I wasn't that sure. As for the civilian authorities supporting this, I know what evidence you're referring to and what a protected witness said. That witness lied and I've already said that here. No one ever supported the bombing of Sarajevo, on the contrary. As a matter of fact, there were decisions to the effect that bombing was impermissible. I think that on the 10th of June this kind of decision was taken by the expanded Presidency to stop the bombing, although it had been provoked. So I know what you're referring to, but that witness was lying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's interesting that you say that, because what I'm actually referring to, Mr. Krajisnik, is something that you said. And I want to turn to P5653 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But before he does that, it would be good to clarify the matter of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 11, it doesn't say that the witness said, "At the time I was not sure, but I listened to them." But I listened to them. I listened to what the army was saying. That is not included. It can be listened to again and you will see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you confirm having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could call up P56 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and we'll resume at 10 past 1.00. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Would that be too much if I ask for a bit shorter break? I would like to finish today. I'm interested in having tomorrow off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, how much longer do you have, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I thought I was going to use most of -- I expected to finish by the end of today, Mr. President, which I thought would pretty much exhaust my time. But I thought I would be using -- I had actually advised Mr. Robinson yesterday that I might finish early, but it doesn't -- I can check in the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, if we have break right now, would we not have difficulty with going until 3.00? I have to consult the Registrar, in terms of tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it mean that you need more than two sessions tomorrow, Mr. Karadzic, for your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, Excellency. I think I would finish in an hour, but tomorrow is my great holiday, St. Michael, the Archangel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, that's been already taken care of. We'll be sitting until 12.30 tomorrow so we have plenty of time. We'll resume at 1.10. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.24 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce Laura Luka [phoen] from Romania who is a legal intern with our Defence team and joining us this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Robinson, if Mr. Tieger would conclude his cross-examination today and if Mr. Karadzic will spend only an hour for his re-direct tomorrow, do we have the next witness available?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. The next witness was scheduled to be Dr. Stakic, but he's not available because his counsel wasn't able to come at this particular point. So we don't have any other witnesses for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure it is a proper use of time, but we'll see how it evolves. Shall we continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just before we adjourned, we had just been about to call up P5683 [sic]. This is a telephone conversation, Mr. Krajisnik, between you and Mr. Motika on the 17th of June, 1995. And as we can see on the first page, make sure you get the -- 56 -- maybe I misspoke. 5653, please. I apparently said "5683." 5653. I'm sorry. Okay, as we see on the first page, there is a call from your office. They get ahold of Motika. He's put through to you. That happens on page 2, both languages. Then you tell him: "I'm interested ... err ... about that very big thing, you know?" And he says: "Yes." And you say: "That thing we didn't use before ..." And he says: "Yes." And you say: "Do you have any of that wheat?" And he says: "Well, there is a little." And you say: "A little?" And he says: "Yes." And you say: "You know what I know." And he says: "I do. There isn't ... an engine." And you say: "Oh, no, not that?" He says: "What?" Said: "More than that. We -- you know, the one that's going -- that brought in a man from Serbia, remember?" And then finally Motika says: "Look, this is a secure line. You can say it. That -- that." Motika says then on page 3 of your language. You say: "Ah, it's secure." So then you go on: "Well, I'm interested in these 'Oganj,' 'Orkan' and the rest." And Motika says: "There's nothing with the Orkan and we adjusted the entire Oganj to 250." And he explains that again: "The entire Oganj has gone to 250." And he says it once more. And he said: "Tell me, is there -- that in Serbia?" He says: "Well, they have it now in Krusik and they may have it in Prva -- and they have it in 'Prva Iskra,' ... perhaps we could request it from there." He wants to know if there are any connections so it can be purchases. He says he has those connections. You say: "Go ahead. Can you arrange for us to set that up? We can try ... down there Visoko ... some retaliation should be done." Motika says: "Well, yeah, we're preparing that right now." You say: "Preparing it?" He says: "Yes." You say: "Go on, prepare it. I've said about that, that if there's anything if it's possible ... do you have an idea for us to use this opportunity because it's very important to retaliate." Motika says: "I propose that it be done in the town." And you say -- now continue on page 4 of your language you say: "Yes, yes." Motika says: "Here in the town." You say: "Sorry?" And he says: "Directly in the town." And you say: "Yes, yes, but it's necessary down there." And he says: "Both down there and here." Your response: "Yes, yes, just go ahead. We'll agree about everything but it's very important down there, where there was a big attack." And it continues on to the next page. Now, this -- these references we see here to 250, no engine, and so forth, this Chamber has received a great deal of evidence about air-bombs which indicates that this discussion, focussing on the use of Oganjs, 250s which are the size of the air-bombs to which Oganj rockets were attacked, no engines, and so forth, reflects that this discussion is about air-bombs; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know and I cannot establish any connection with air-bombs. I'm not versed in this kind of technical matters. Oganj and other names are completely dissociated from air-bombs and I'm hearing this from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if you and Motika weren't talking about the use of FAB-250 air-bombs to which Oganjs were affixed as propellants, what were you -- what kind of weaponry were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I'm not a technically minded person when it comes to weapons. Oganj is something completely different, it's a rocket and has nothing to do with air-bomb. That's what I know as a layperson. I did not discuss air-bombs. I was discussing a particular case and I know what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You're discussing with Motika your interest in rockets; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a long barrel, that's what it's called, Oganj. It's probably called Oganj and that was the weapon that I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Whatever weaponry you're talking about and -- first of all, you acknowledge that Motika was talking about 250s, he's explaining that the Oganjs had gone for the 250s. That's what he told you contemporaneously?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still don't know what this 250 means. I heard it from them, that Oganj was a barrel-shaped means that was produced in Travnik and that it was very efficient in combat. This is what I heard from them as an ordinary person and this is what I heard on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So you're not disputing that Motika is talking about the transformation of the supply of Oganj rockets to the 250s for the use -- for use as air-bombs. You're just saying you don't know what he meant?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm disputing that I still don't know what it means. You think that I was discussing Oganj. I wasn't discussing air-bombs. I am not an expert in that. I know what I asked for, what I was talking about. I wasn't talking about air-bombs. If it was him who raised the issue of air-bombs, then so be it. I am not versed in these technical matters, otherwise I would have been able to give you an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So in this conversation, according to you, are you talking about retaliation through the use of air-bombs, Oganjs, or some other weaponry system?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a ferocious attack from Visoko at Ilijas at the time. Since this is a neighbouring municipality, they came in panic asking for help to stop the attack because there were lots of civilian casualties, the Serbs. I asked Motika if anything more powerful can be used in order to deter the attack because there was another attack in the pipeline as a last-ditch attempt on the part of the Muslim policy to, as they put it, expel the Serbs totally and to lift the blockade of Sarajevo but also of Central Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. What were you referring to when you said "do you have any of that wheat" in the early part of discussion before Motika told you that the line was secure?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought that wheat referred to shells for launchers or mines. It is closely connected but it's disassociated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how routinely do you claim you and Motika were in contact about issues related to weaponry systems? You'll agree that this is obviously not the first time you spoke to him about such a matter?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the area from where I came and Motika worked in a factory close to Serbian Sarajevo, which is my native place. I cannot say I contacted with him often, but we did speak to each other on a number of occasions. It was a private relationship and the local population was constantly asking for assistance and I had no other recourse than to ask someone else for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's the same explanation you gave during your trial about your repeated contacts with military figures. You insisted repeatedly that it was purely for a matter of a kind of private inquiry from an interested citizen, even though the contemporaneous conversations captured in the intercepts reflected that you were intervening in matters for the purpose of getting action taken on the ground, either to relieve people who were under combat pressure or to determine what had happened in response to actions taken by Bosnian Serb forces. Do you remember that? Do you remember that? Remember the whole series of intercepts with you and Garic and others, where you're inquiring about what's going on. I need to know. Following up on those calls, and you tried to dismiss them as simply your private, curious inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it curiosity. It was a necessity. I was a deputy from the Serbian Sarajevo or Sarajevo, and during the war that was a Serb-controlled territory. A large number of politicians, including members of my family, tried privately through me to gain assistance and protection because they were under threat. And most definitely, privately and for their own reasons, I was even sometimes criticised of being -- intervening on behalf of Sarajevo. On several times I pleaded with the army in order to improve the situation, in order to protect the population. But the sole reason for that was because I hail from that area. Although I was a political functionary at the republican level, I never displayed such a level of interest for Banja Luka, for example, and perhaps I should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to turn, in the interests of time, to some things you spent a great deal of time with on your examination-in-chief, and that was the Cutileiro Plan. I think it's fair to say you emphasised that not only in your examination-in-chief but also your cross-examination. And you attempted -- you asserted that the Bosnian Serbs had been assured or promised by the European community that they would get their own entity and that the European representative prepared a map which the strategic objectives simply followed, and that was your explanation for any number of things that we looked at that the Bosnian Serbs did; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the reality, Mr. Krajisnik, is that although negotiations were conducted under the auspices of the European community, nothing was promised to the Bosnian Serbs, as we can see reflected in P952, which is a letter in June from Mr. Cutileiro to Mr. Karadzic. And if we could call that up, please. As we can see, this is dated the 12th of June, 1992, and in the third paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be beneficial if there is a translation so that I can follow and subsequently to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'll get you to the third paragraph in a minute, if I can, through a synopsis. If the Defence feels like it's not sufficient to contextualise the comment in the third paragraph, they can make that known. So the first paragraph thanks Mr. Karadzic for his letter of the 5th of June, points to a comment by Lord Carrington that the only way to peace in Bosnia is through negotiation. A political settlement is essential. And that's been emphasised in a UN Resolution. Carrington went on to say: "'... there is absolutely no question of the Conference, or for that matter the international community, endorsing a policy of 'fait accompli.' Territorial claims which have been pursued by force are totally unacceptable.'" Now, me stop there, since you asked to read it. There, that's a reference to what the Bosnian Serbs were doing, that is, going on the offensive to liberate, conquer, seize, or control territory; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this refers to Serbs specifically. This is a general statement. We accepted --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Krajisnik please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first paragraph which speaks about the territories taken by force, that coincided with our position and we agreed to that. There is even a document signed by Mr. Karadzic that this is exactly our view and that we accepted that and that was incorporated in nearly all the agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The second paragraph refers to Cutileiro's intention to reconvene the talks as soon as the questions of the airport, free passage of humanitarian relief, and Serbian artillery around Sarajevo are resolved through the mediation of UNPROFOR. And he urges Mr. Karadzic to do everything in his power to facilitate a satisfactory solution. Now we get to the third paragraph where Cutileiro says: "Let me add one thing ... the European community has not made any promises to you. What happened, as you well know, is that talks on future constitutional arrangements for Bosnia and Herzegovina among the three main political parties ... under my chairmanship, were established by Lord Carrington in early February. On the 18th of March, we reached agreement on a set of principles. The validity of that agreement, however, can only be upheld if borders and competences of the constituent units be defined by negotiated consensus and not by force, and if 'ethnically cleansed' territories be restored to their ante-bellum ethnical compositions." And he concludes by saying: "I'm sure you realise that it is in your interest to do everything from your side to ... achieve those results." And Ambassador Cutileiro testified here as a witness for Dr. Karadzic. He verified that letter, and there was never a suggestion in his testimony by him or by anyone else during the course of his testimony that the international community promised or told the Serbs that they would simply be given their own ethnic unit. So I put it to you, Mr. Krajisnik, that your claim is essentially an attempt to justify your military conquests of the areas that you wanted for the [indiscernible] which you were unable to get by negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try once again to interpret what I said in this trial. I said that the first information that we would be given our national entity was received from Mr. Milosevic. Prior to that, there were talks with Mr. Carrington and other international representatives. That what Mr. Milosevic said was true was to the effect that you are going to get your own entity in exchange for giving up on Yugoslavia. He confirmed that to Mr. Cutileiro when he came, and at the time we had an endorsement of the European community because he presented these principles exactly commensurate with what we had received previously as information. This is the truth. Mr. Cutileiro, that is true, never said explicitly: I am guaranteeing you that you are going to get this and that except for one thing, and I think that you have it in the documents. On the 17th of March, in a meeting where we were, Mr. Cutileiro said in response to our question: Are we going to get our constituent unit? He said: Not one, you will get more than one. And we said: We only want one. He then went to talk to the Muslim side and he said they agreed, and you can find it in the documents. In this meeting he said: You're going to get your entity. It is not a promise. This was the adopted policy by the European community and that is the genuine truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So notwithstanding what Mr. Cutileiro said in a contemporaneous letter, that this was all about negotiations and dependent upon consensus among those parties, notwithstanding what he told this Trial Chamber when he came to testify 20 years later, you maintain that that's wrong and that instead you were acting on the assurance by the European community that you had an ethnic entity?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect for Mr. Cutileiro, what I said a minute ago is true. He said on the 17th: You are going to get your national entity, and the entire agreement was based on that sentence of his. The Muslims and the Croats were aware of that and they set up the exactly same principles. That's what he said. And there was never any doubt or dispute that this promise existed, and this was verified in the Dayton Agreement. Everybody was to get their own entity except for the Vance-Owen Plan, where there was an attempt to deviate from the originally accepted principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you also referred repeatedly to the so-called -- or what you termed as the Cutileiro map, something that you called the Cutileiro map but Mr. Cutileiro didn't nor did anybody else. Mr. Cutileiro testified to the contrary, that there was a map annexed to the agreement which showed the relative majority in each municipality and that that would be the basis of the working group; that is, it showed the current municipality structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it shaded in, according to the ethnic group, which of the ethnic groups had an absolute or a relative majority there. That map's in evidence as P782. You saw it in your case. It's the one with -- drawn in with the cross-hatching and the stripes. And Mr. Cutileiro further indicated that that map was a preliminary map, so much so that we decided to create a Working Group, a Working Group that was never created. And that's at T33965. Now, that was testimony that he offered at the behest of Dr. Karadzic. Mr. Cutileiro never testified about the existence or creation of another map, never suggested there was another map, and Dr. Karadzic never asked him about another map or suggested that one in any way existed. So I submit that the map that you presented here in court, that coloured map published in 1996 that's in Cyrillic, is not the Cutileiro map. The only Cutileiro map is the one reflected in P782.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you are not right. There is proof here - and I saw it while preparing for this testimony - the "Politika" daily of 19th March published this map. Please find this document here and show it. If it was published on the 19th of March, then it doesn't stand that it does not exist. You have it in the documents; I have it on my laptop. And I claim that there are two maps. Your map, which you referred to as Cutileiro's one, was made by the late Mr. Darwin, and it only represented which ethnic community was in majority and where. Before our 12th of May Assembly in Brussels, the line on the Una was drawn up for the first time, and that is why we introduced as one of our strategic objectives the border on the Una. If you find this document, you will see that this is true and I'm referring to the "Politika" daily of the 19th of March. I hope I'm not mistaken. I think this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D302.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Cutileiro also confirmed an article he wrote in which he stated that following the breakdown of negotiations after 18 March, the Bosnian Serbs felt confirmed in their paranoid view of history and went brutally on the offensive. That's found at T33953. And he accepted that the control of municipalities such as Zvornik, Bratunac, Vlasenica, Srebrenica, Rogatica, Visegrad, all reflected as Muslim majority in the map annexed to the statement of principles, shifted as a result of the conflict, that's at 33969. And that's exactly what he was referring to in the letter of June 12th as well that we looked at a moment ago; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Cutileiro had in mind. I can say that when the war started, each municipality at its local level in this all-out war was in conflict. And whoever was stronger militarily was victorious in such a municipality. We lost some territories but we acquired other territories. That was a war among three peoples. There was no guidance. There was no connection with the municipal levels. People in Sarajevo were saying: We don't even know if Karadzic is alive, let alone that there was someone pulling the strings from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, somewhat related to this subject was your repeated emphasis that your focus on the strategic objectives, your repetition about the strategic objectives, in your meetings with the military were simply a reflection of the fact that it was public knowledge because, as you said, it had been publicly announced and there was nothing new, everybody knew that the strategic objectives were public, et cetera. And you tried to do the same thing in the Popovic case. You said that the annunciation of the strategic objectives at the 16th Assembly was a way of informing the international community and the public at large about our positions since all the meetings and sessions were public. That's found at transcript 21583 through 84 of the transcript in the Popovic case. Can you confirm that that was your position in Popovic or do you wish to see the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say I wasn't really following so well what you want. When I testified in the Popovic case, I believe it's reflected correctly in the transcript. I didn't check but I believe that it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And the point here, Mr. Krajisnik, is that you were saying to the Judges in the Popovic case that the annunciation of the strategic objectives was simply the public exposure, the public exposition of the ongoing negotiations, and so it would be disseminated because all your sessions were public. And then you continue to offer that same explanation here, that the strategic -- that notwithstanding your repeated admonitions and focus on the strategic objectives in your meetings and Dr. Karadzic's meetings with the leadership of the VRS, that didn't have any significance because it was somehow just your reminding them that everybody knew about the negotiations. That's essentially what I was pointing you to. Now, first of all, the reality is that the 16th Session was not an open session; it was closed. And we can look first to -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a P number I should have memorised by now, but I see that nobody else jumped up with their own recollections. It's P956.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's a transcript of the 16th Session.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you don't have to bother. It was a closed session in part. I remember that. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Okay. And you were reminded of that in the Popovic case after you first asserted that -- and tried to explain the strategic objectives as being the public dissemination of the negotiating position. You were then confronted with evidence that the session was indeed closed, and then you acknowledged it had been closed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The session, a part of it was closed and I can also tell you why that was closed, not because of the six strategic goals but because of something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you're saying -- was it closed -- okay. What part of the session do you claim was closed, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. You can see it from the minutes. It's easy to establish that. I don't know it off the top of my head, but it wasn't because of the six strategic goals that had already been announced to the public, to the international community. It was not a secret matter. Our platform, the six strategic goals, and the map, all of that was already publicly announced and I can also provide evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What -- where was -- who publicly announced it before the 16th Assembly Session, according to you? Or what document reflects the public provision of the six strategic goals before the 16th Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say "before." What I said was that they were discussed at the 16th Session, and then on the 9th of June you can find the Presidency minutes for that, where it says these goals should be sent to the international community and our map, meaning the map, the map. We sent it all to the international community and publish openly. And so the secretary made a mistake. He was thinking of publishing it in the Official Gazette, and then when he saw that he made a decision he crossed it out, and then instead of a conclusion he said "decision." And then a few days later when they were making a new report on the work, the new secretary put that in and that is why there is that problem about the subsequent publication of the strategic goals as a decision, but it had already been sent to the international community. You can read the minutes and you can see that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't hear you because of overlapping, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that the witness is referring to is 0428.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He's referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You referred explicitly to the June 9th Presidency session. Okay. So, first, you said in Popovic that the session was open and so was the exposure of the six strategic goals. Now -- then you said it was closed. And now you say: Well, it was disseminated after the decision that's reflected in the June 9th, 1992, Presidency session minutes. But the fact is that the strategic goals were not published in the Official Gazette until the latter part of 1993, and that happened when someone came to you, according to you, and to note that there was no record of the strategic goals anywhere and that something should be published so that it could be reflected in the official records. And that's what you said in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said in the Popovic case is correct because while I was preparing for my appeal I found documents which explain all of that. Mr. President, if you like, I can provide the whole chronology of how this document came about and why it was subsequently published, how it was publicised, and that it was not a secret document of any kind. If you permit me, I will easily explain that. At this Tribunal there are all these documents that I sent to the Prosecution and to each Judge in my case, and I also have it on CD and I can easily submit that to you tomorrow if you wish, all of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If Mr. Karadzic is interested in. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As long as we're talking about Presidency sessions, I wanted to raise one other matter with you, Mr. Krajisnik. During the course of your testimony in your case, you had opportunity to look at the conclusions from a session of the government held on the 10th of June, and that's P1092, if we could call that up. If we could turn to item 6 which is on page 3 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. That reflects the conclusion that the Ministry of Justice should make a report about prisoners: "This report should pay special attention on treatment of civilian population, prisoners of war, accommodation, food, et cetera. The report would be considered by the government, after which it would be submitted to the Presidency of the Republic." Now, you testified in your case that on the basis of this document and on the basis of these conclusions, one could infer that information about maltreatment of prisoners reached the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that, Mr. Krajisnik? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I was waiting for a question. I didn't understand that as a question. If it's not a problem, could you please repeat it. I'm not sure I understand what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure, and I'm sorry I wasn't more clearer. I just want you to confirm that you testified in your case that on the basis of this document, on the basis of these conclusions, one can infer that information about maltreatment of prisoners reached the government?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, when I read it, I don't see it. But if it states so there, there must be a reason that I said that. Perhaps somebody put an additional question to me. We're talking about the treatment of the civilian population, prisoners of war, accommodation, food, and so on and so forth. So from what I can see here, you cannot see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll read you what you said at 2441 [sic]: Were you at this time," we're talking about the 10th of June, "had you received or heard any concerns that prisoners of war were being maltreated at the hands of Serbs in an unacceptable or inappropriate way?" You said: "The answer is no. No, I am so convinced that I was never informed of any such thing. Had I been informed, I certainly would have intervened in order to have an analysis carried out, if I can put it that way. However, on the basis of this," and you're looking at the 10 June minutes at the time, "I can infer that a similar type of information reached the government and then the government sent a commission of its own to investigate these rumours ...," et cetera. Okay. So that was the position you took in your trial, that one could see from -- one could infer from this, that the government had heard something about and was seeking a report specifically about how civilians and prisoners of war were being treated?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't state it -- say something different today. The government on the basis of this knew about the prisoners and was asking for information about prisoners of war. I assume that some reports reached the government, and prompted by those rumours or indicia the government sought some kind of information and a report of sorts was made about the treatment of persons of different ethnicities in prison. Probably there was some other issues there as well which are not relevant to what we are discussing right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you also explain that you didn't know -- you didn't have such information or -- that the -- of the type the government had because this was just something the government decided on its own independently; correct? That was your testimony? First, before you explain it, if you can confirm or not that that was your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. But if you want me to explain what I said in this testimony, that I can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you still -- do you maintain now that this was something the government did on its own independently and that's why you didn't have such information, because the information they had that's reflected in these conclusions was something that -- and that triggered this call for the Ministry of Justice to make a report was something that only the government had?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer at that trial was that I was not informed about criminals of war or war crimes, but if any rumours or indicia appeared, a reaction ensued immediately. It's possible that there was some sort of information and that on the basis of that the government reacted. Possibly. I don't know that. I know that every time a rumour popped up there would be a reaction. It's possible that Mr. Djeric was at our extended meeting and that this was discussed and then it was said: Let the government make a report and say whether this was true or not. That would always be our action and -- reaction. And I testified to that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you just put your finger on exactly the point I was going to make, and that is the following: It's not only possible that Mr. Djeric was at your extended meeting; that's in fact exactly how it happened, that there was a Presidency session at which Mr. Djeric was tasked to do this, and that's found at P1093, page 2, that the government then submit a report on prisoners with proposed measures.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. That means that the meeting was there, the government -- the task was issued, the government reacted, and that's it. It's possible. I mean, I forgot that particular case, but it wasn't that case. Maybe there were other cases, but there would always be actions to investigate, establish, see what it was, and to have a report done and to punish the perpetrators. That I know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I know that's the position you're taking now, now that you have the range of documents in front of you. But I just want to be clear on what happened in the Krajisnik case when you were testifying for the first time. And then you wanted to say two things. Number one, you never had any information that there was a problem with prisoners and civilians being held; and number two, it may be that the government found out about it but they immediately launched an inquiry, but they did all that independently, on their own. That was your testimony initially, right, and that's what you just confirmed a moment ago, I think, that you said that first when asked?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prosecutor, sir, then and before, I always spoke the truth the way I knew it. Always when an information would turn up, the information was always an assumption and the reaction would be: It's not true, but let the organs investigate and get the information. That's the true. If I said that I perhaps never heard of a crime, I did not. Perhaps I heard about some assumptions, speculations, indicia. There was some propaganda, lies on all sides during the war. So this is not something that is in collision. I'm simply telling you how after a certain piece of information I can round off my thought, and what I said in my trial was confirmed. There was no firm news about crimes. There were some indications, perhaps rumours, but never definite information. There were always lies and rumours in war time. Let me give you an example. You saw that on the 7th of August there was a Presidency session, and Mr. Karadzic approved visits to all prisons for journalists and international mediators. Had we known that there were crimes there, we would not have approved it. We would have postponed that permission. It was not something that was done maliciously. Simply, we said: We don't have any information about crimes. You are free to go and visit any of the prisoners -- any of the prisons, to all representatives of the Red Cross, the international intermediaries, there were no crimes that we were aware of at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I tender 24438 and 24441 to the portions that I referred to at length?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We haven't looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I know, Mr. President, but I mean, we can look at them but I did recite them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can do -- if you are tendering, I would like to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. 24441, please, of 65 ter 25522. If we look at lines 11 through -- 11 and 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "However, on the basis of this I can infer that a similar type of information reached the government ...," et cetera. And if we can turn to 24438. "Can you say whether at this time, this was the 10th of June, were you aware of any special concerns in relation to treatment of, first of all, civilian population?" And you said: "This was something that the government decided on its own independently because it came under its competence and authority ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I tender those portions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add them to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at that time, June 10th, we've seen evidence -- very recently, in fact, we've reviewed such evidence that by that time there were thousands and thousands and thousands of prisoners being held in the Krajina alone, as reflected in repeated daily combat reports of the 1 KK, for example. Now, those people were rounded up at the end of May/beginning of June. They continued to languish in detention facilities in the Krajina and elsewhere throughout June, throughout July, and it wasn't until August when the international community gained access to Omarska and publicised it that any action was taken with respect to those detention facilities, Mr. Krajisnik; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't confirm your entire explanation. Perhaps it was confirmed during this trial, but at that time, if we're talking about that time, there was a blockade that Krajina was isolated and none of us had that information. You had witnesses here, they didn't know in Banja Luka what was going on in Omarska, and then a delegation went and was flabbergasted to see what was going on, never mind us in Pale knowing what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the 2nd of June Mr. Brdjanin told Mr. Karadzic personally, asked him personally, for a position about prisoners. That was one day after reports from the 1 KK reflect the seizing and detention of 7.000 people from Kozarac alone. Dr. Karadzic had access to information from the military, didn't he, and information from the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not in dispute that -- whether it was known on all three sides that there were prisons in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was general knowledge. The problem was the treatment in those prisons. I assert, I'm convinced that Karadzic didn't know that either. He would have told me. I know definitely that I did not know it and Mr. Karadzic did not know it either. Had he known, he would have informed us. Had he known, he would have informed us about it. I assume so. And as for the letter by Mr. Brdjanin, he probably explained what he was seeking and what reply he got. I mean, I really cannot comment on that because I'm not really knowledgeable about that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me focus for a moment, then, on the reliability of what you explained to us you knew or didn't know. You testified in your trial in 2006 that as for Koricanske Stijene, that is, the murder of more than 200 unarmed Bosnian Muslim men at Vlasic mountain, you never heard of it: "As for Koricanske Stijene, I never heard of it ..." And you said: "I only heard about Koricanske Stijene in The Hague ..." That's found at 24636, lines 15 and lines 1 through 2. That was your testimony under oath before this institution in 2006; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct and I explained that to you and I explained to you the things that were misinterpreted by SRNA, our news agency. I can explain what I said then. What I said then is correct and I claim that to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, one of the witnesses in this case, a witness called by Dr. Karadzic, was former Minister of Defence Subotic. And he testified, that's found at transcript pages 40104 through 40109, that he was dispatched to the Krajina following events at Koricanske Stijene and that he briefed the Presidency in detail about what happened there. That is, he came back from being dispatched to the Krajina, and when he reported to the Presidency he told them all about Koricanske Stijene. And that's reflected in P0303, a meeting of September 1st that reflects his return from the Krajina, his briefing the Presidency members, and your attendance at that session.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Subotic testified at my trial too, and if you take a look at that, you will see that he said that when this meeting was held when he was supposed to go to the Krajina when he received that information, I was not present. I explained why I was not present. You will remember that. On the 21st of August, I believe, my wife was seriously wounded in Pale. I was with her in Belgrade at the military medical academy and she died on the 23rd. All that time, while these activities were underway, I was not present at that meeting. You saw the SRNA report there which is wrong. When I was in Belgrade when she died, they wrote that I received some delegation. That was completely false, a lie. I don't know why, maybe misinterpreted seven days' difference. I was not informed then and I did not know. And on the 1st of September I don't think that it was then that he informed the Presidency. In my presence he did not inform the Presidency about that, perhaps before that, between the 21st and the 1st of September, maybe at some meeting when I was not present. It took seven days. I brought my wife back from Belgrade, buried her. All of that happened then. So the statement I gave then is quite correct, and that was confirmed by Mr. Subotic when he testified in my case, that I was not present at that meeting when he spoke about what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the meeting at which he was dispatched. I'm talking about his report back on the situation. We also heard from Mr. Aviljas, another Defence witness, who also participated in meetings related to Koricanske Stijene and he said everybody in RS knew about that. And he meant everybody. He didn't just mean the top leadership who would be expecting to know about this stuff, he meant that this was no secret. So were you the only person who didn't hear about this, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm telling you, at that time, I'm telling you what the situation was, what my situation was, and I tell you I was not informed about that and I was not dealing with Koricanske Stijene. Had somebody informed me -- I mean, Mr. Subotic said that he gave a task to the MUP and the 1st Krajina Corps to investigate that and to punish the perpetrators. Well, had that been the case, that would have been a normal sequence of events; however, I did not attend that meeting and I did not receive that information. I did not attend that meeting. It doesn't matter. There should have been a request to punish the perpetrators, to investigate and punish the perpetrators, and that's what I heard from Mr. Subotic. You can check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Last issue, Mr. Krajisnik, last question in fact. You told this Court in response to questions from Mr. Karadzic that you believed that -- or it was your impression that Mr. Holbrooke did not believe that Mr. Karadzic was guilty. So somehow you called upon whatever contact you had with the late Mr. Holbrooke to suggest that he had formed a view of Mr. Karadzic's innocence, and in that regard I'd like to call up 65 ter 25654. And in an interview that took place at the time of Mr. Karadzic's arrest, Mr. Holbrooke was interviewed by "Spiegel" and asked what that meant to him. He said he was overjoyed. This was bringing to justice one of the worst, most evil men in the world. First for his responsibility for hundreds of thousands of deaths. He notes that he believed in racial superiority even though Muslims and Serbs were really basically the same ethnicity. And finally ends up saying he would have made a good Nazi. This is a more accurate reflection, is it not, of Mr. Holbrooke's view of Dr. Karadzic's guilt or innocence than the impressions you offered here under oath in response to Mr. Karadzic's urging?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to repeat this. In my view, at that moment it was irrelevant for Mr. Holbrooke whether Karadzic was guilty or not. He thought that the indictment against Karadzic was an instrument for implementing the Dayton Agreement, and if Karadzic were to go illegal, if I can put it that way or leave all the offices held, that would have meant that he would have accomplished his missions. What Mr. Holbrooke said in this interview, that was not his opinion, that was not his view and he never showed that in any way. Nothing would have indicated this. I can just explain this in the following way: At the time when he was working on the agreement, he was in power. And after that, he wasn't in power. And then he was trying to justify why he had reached this agreement. It's not that he reached this agreement without anybody's consent. I saw him making phone calls, and he said for Mr. Karadzic the Hague Tribunal is the past, and that is correct. And there is also other information stating that Mrs. Albright said the same things to Mrs. Plavsic. That's contained in her book too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that and conclude my cross-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see the need to admit it. The relevant part was put to the witness and he answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Speaker.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you whether you remember what the late Holbrooke said about rhetoric when you were parting, when the oral part of the agreement had been reached?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Holbrooke said it is very important that Mr. Karadzic does not appear in public, does not make public statements, et cetera, that was my understanding. And as Mr. Bildt said that he should go into the basement, not be a public person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did he say anything about their rhetoric in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said -- please, you have to understand, this is an agreement. However, in public we will have to be speaking differently because this would have been working against the Hague Tribunal which would not have been right because it would have meant that we as a state do not support the Hague Tribunal, whereas we do that publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on with the most recent things. Can you tell us, Mr. Speaker, according to the constitution, what are the powers of the Assembly, what are the powers of the Presidency or the president, and did you have to be informed ex officio about crimes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Ex officio, nobody was supposed to inform me about crimes, not even you. You didn't have to be informed about crimes either. According to procedure, it was important to report that to institutions that were in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When would they have to inform me, in which case would they have to inform me if they had already informed the institutions concerned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's only logical.
