If a certain institution were passive, if it would not want to take measures, if it would refuse to take measures, then those providing the information would have the right to inform the prime minister, the government, even the president of the republic as the highest executive body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, in our system and I believe in other systems too, where is policy created? How is policy created and how is it implemented?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Top-level policy, international policy, is pursued by the Presidency and the president. The Assembly passes documents and the government implements policy. So if the Presidency adopts a document or if a -- or if the government adopts a document, as far as the pursuit of policy is concerned, that is done by the executive and by certain ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 89 of today's transcript you were asked what -- actually, it's from 87. It says that you said that the government carried out an investigation independently. Who else could have conducted an investigation in addition to the government, or rather, its ministries?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: By inertia I said this, because the Prosecutor was trying to say that now all of us were supposed to be conducting this investigation, the Speaker of the Assembly, the president of the republic, and everybody else, and I said that this was autonomous, without any kind of initiative or some kind of joint meeting. That is what the government did. That was the task of the government. That was the task of the ministries because the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of the Interior are within the government. And these ministries are in charge of carrying out policy, of course, through the prosecutor's office and through courts of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On pages 84 onwards -- actually, before that, did you attend that government session that you were asked about in relation to the government's questions about the treatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can be seen here that I did not attend this government meeting because on that same day, perhaps in the morning, there was a session, I mean this consultative session, of the National Security Council. We all attended that, perhaps in the morning, and then in the afternoon the government looked at these problems on its own perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If the government is seeking information about crimes from the ground, if you will, then this poor treatment of prisoners, would that be part of our policy?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. That was a constant task of the ministry and of the government as a whole, to bear this in mind for treatment to be correct. There were even these instructions that were adopted by the government, that is to say how the prison authorities would behave towards prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But it seems to me that I was confused when I was putting my question. If prisoners were ill-treated, or rather, if that was part of our policy, would the government have to ask us or the grass roots?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they would ask us. They would say: Why are you doing that if that is policy? It's against the Geneva Conventions and everything else. However, if somebody - how do I put this? - is pursuing an erroneous policy and if there is ill-treatment and if the political leadership thinks that people should be treated properly, then of course they should ask people at the grass roots: Why are you doing that? And then let us inform the top leadership, let us take political measures, and let us have the organs in charge file criminal reports, prosecute this, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 83 Mr. Tieger suggested that, as regards strategic objectives, they were not discussed between the 12th of May and the autumn of 1993 -- or rather, between the 12th of May and the time when they were made public. You and I, did we have an interview? Were we interviewed on Republika Srpska TV with the late Risto Djogo in January or February 1993?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I was reminded of this interview in these materials, but before that interview I mentioned the 9th of June when we publicly concluded -- I mean, these principles. The six -- actually, objectives should be made public, sent to the international representatives, together with a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked and it was often mentioned the meaning of strategic objective number 3. Do you recall on that programme? And I'm referring to document that is in evidence. I'm just looking for its number. How did we explain to the public in this programme the significance and the meaning of the strategic objective number 3, that is to say the Drina and its nature?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, we did exactly as I interpreted before this Tribunal. You said on that occasion that we allow for certain enclaves to exist, I think that was mentioned in the Assembly, and I'm talking about Muslim enclaves that would enjoy all rights. Our entire policy, I'm going to repeat it once again irrespective of this, was to use our resources not to have the Drina as a psychological burden on the shoulders of the Serbian people. It should have been a porous border without passport, without border posts, and we managed to achieve that only later because all links with Serbia were subsequently allowed. No passports are required. There are no border posts, and all of this was done not to the detriment of either the Muslims or the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have D1934 in e-court, please, both in the Serbian and in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this text. Try to remember whether this was the programme when the two of us were interviewed by members of the public.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this interview, maybe not all the details, but I do remember it. I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 3 in Serbian and I believe it's the same page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this part -- I'm afraid we need the next page, 3, and the time-line is 2.41. There's something wrong here. That's not the right page as the one that I have. I'm sorry, I have an abbreviated version, so it would be on page 28, which means that I have just a few pages here in court, whereas there are many more on the screen. Please look at your response where you spoke about the fourth strategic objective, that is to say the Neretva valley. Can you please read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I think that the Neretva valley was the most manipulated subject and the left bank of the Neretva because lots of misinformation was disseminated as if we had sold it to Herceg-Bosna, that is to say to the Croats. One of our strategic goals was to have a border between eastern and western Herzegovina, between these two provinces, should be the Neretva river and that we would persist on that in our negotiations."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the next page, please. Page number 30 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the last question posed by the anchor about the border between Serbia and the Republika Srpska, how it's going to work and whether the world knew that there was no border between Croatia and Herceg-Bosna, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me read it. Radovan Karadzic responded: "Thus, well I think that the Muslim leadership, when they requested that borders be controlled by the central government, referred to the borders between Herzegovina and Croatia, as those borders don't exist, where there are no restrictions, rather than to the Drina border. We'll never allow, and that is one of the strategic aims we adopted at the Assembly, we'll never allow the border running along Serbian territories to become real, restrictive, although that was the case for a while, because of the economic relationship was such that it had to be imposed, but things will change. Whichever way we deal with it, Serbian areas in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina will enjoy great freedom of economic and other communications with whomever they choose. This is in accordance with the Lisbon document and other documents ..." and this is where it ends.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please. We can keep the English but we need the next page in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Lisbon document and other documents, that is in accordance with the current European trend. The Germans and the French have that freedom, Alsace and Lorraine have that freedom, those rights will have Serbs living on both sides of the Drina ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There are quite a few more instructive things, but let us go back -- well, never mind. All right, so in January or February when this interview took place, did we publicly speak about the strategic objectives and explained what we meant by them? Did this imply unification with Serbia or what Europe has in the aftermath of the Maastricht Agreement, that is to say soft borders?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is quite clear that this corresponds exactly to what I said in my testimony, that we wanted a porous border without border posts and customs control in the sense that is usually perceived between two hostile countries. This was a true reflection of our policy and this was supported by Mr. Izetbegovic. I would refer the Chamber to an extract, or rather, a piece of evidence in my case which is a quotation from Mr. Izetbegovic's memoirs, where he says exactly that the Serbs must not feel confined, that they must not show passports on the Drina, that this border must be porous, that they can freely pass across it, and that no one should feel that border to be a burden.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we again have page 29 in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You spoke about people being upset and alarmed once they hear that certain area would be given to someone else. Look at the last entry of Radovan Karadzic on this page, where our enemies are spreading rumours about some things being sold out, that Karadzic gave away Vogosca and Ilijas which was followed by an offensive. First they softened the defence and then it was followed by an offensive. Did you have that in mind?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But also another example which refers to the Neretva. In the course of adopting the objective goals on the [indiscernible] of May, the JNA held the Neretva river valley and the access to sea; however, after one of our visits, either on the 5th or 6th of May, you, I, and Mr. Koljevic were in Herzegovina. On that occasion, Mr. Koljevic inadvertently and carelessly informed people over the radio that we had agreed with the Croats in Graz to have the left bank of the Neretva given to the Serbs and the right one to the Croats; however, that the Croats did not agree with that. They wanted the dividing line to be on the Titova Street --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the interpreters didn't follow you. Please start from when you referred to Titova Street. They wanted to -- the dividing line to be on the Titova Street, and then please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best. I'm sorry. Mr. Koljevic carelessly said, or rather, interpreted our agreement with the Croats reached in Graz. He said that there were certain differences between our position and their position in the sense that we demanded a border to be on the Neretva river, whereas the Croats wanted a small belt on the left bank up to Titova Street to belong to them. And he said that we had to reach an agreement with Croats. On that same day, whilst we were in Nevesinje where we stayed, five young Serb men were killed, combatants from a unit that went on its own initiative, because this was still an armed people, to liberate a Serbian village, and as a result they were killed, which means that all these households were extinguished. This caused an uproar among the citizens, this statement of his, and immediately rumours were spread that the negotiating team was selling out the river Neretva valley, that is to say that the politicians from both the valley and from the top leadership were prepared to give up on the Neretva and the result was that the army withdrew from that area, just as the army withdrew from the Prevlaka and the seashore. And I can confirm that whenever such statements or such news appeared, that softened the front line and the people were manning the front line. People would simply retreat from those areas, which means that we did not have an advantage in terms of the size of the territory. It was, rather, a burden for us so it was not easy for us to create a map if you have a big territory. Only after the Dayton Accords when our territory was reduced to 45 per cent, it was very easy to participate in the negotiations. It is a paradox, but it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked today why, or rather, with -- about the promise or the offer of the international community for us to get a constituent unit. Did we accept unconditionally for Bosnia-Herzegovina to leave Yugoslavia? What was our condition in that regard ?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in this trial as well, that a promise was made. It was not a condition of ours. It was a promise made by Mr. Milosevic and by others as well that we had to give up Yugoslavia in return for a constituent unit in Bosnia. That was made quite clear to us, and that is why before that we organised a plebiscite. We all voted for remaining in Yugoslavia; however, quite simply, after that we had to change our policy, our real policy. If we cannot have Yugoslavia, we shall have our constituent unit within Bosnia and we shall recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina as a complex state and that was the reason why we forgot about Yugoslavia and accepted Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state. After we gave our agreement, Montenegro decided to form a new Yugoslavia, but not before we gave our consent to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 27 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you something about a position on that page. Did we strive to defeat - and I mean you yourself, among others - to defeat Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can categorically say that our policy was not to defeat Croats and Muslims, even if we had been able to because our policy was separation, separation meant that we wanted to have our own constituent unit within Bosnia, which means internal demarcation. Why? Now, Your Honours and Mr. President, let me remind you that we were out-voted in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and due to that we could not allow for this policy to continue. That's why we said: All right, you Muslims and Croats don't want to remain in Yugoslavia; however, we do not trust you and we do not want to remain with you in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You out-voted us even before the war. One can only imagine how you're going to out-vote us once we remained alone in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So our policy was to separate from them, not to defeat them. So let us make an arbitrary assumption. Let's say that the Muslims capitulated, as well as the Croats, and that Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krajisnik please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are speaking too fast. Let us assume Muslims capitulated, start from there slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to explain why we preferred separation. For example, if we had defeated Muslims and Croats, Bosnia would have been an independent state already recognised. What would happen? The same thing would happen. We would be out-voted. We were in favour of Yugoslavia and the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina within Yugoslavia perhaps divided into economic regions. Once Yugoslavia disappeared and once we were put under the jurisdiction of this coalition that out-voted us, we said that we cannot be sure that we are not going to be out-voted again in the future. And you can see that happening even nowadays after the Dayton Accord. That's our situation. So in response to your question, we did not want to defeat the Muslims. We wanted an honest division. We wanted to have our constituent unit comprising only Serbian areas. We failed to achieve that. Some of our ethnic territories remained within the Muslim/Croat entity, whereas other parts, that is to say parts belonging to the Muslims and Croats, remained within Republika Srpska. But generally speaking, the ethnic division was successfully and ultimately implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this, Djogo says -- actually, a viewer from Pale says: Why doesn't Radovan Karadzic order the liberation of Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Please, next page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this your last question in relation to this clip? Otherwise we will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency, but there is a complementary intercept that I wanted to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. About -- I'm asking whether to adjourn now or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay, we can adjourn now and I will continue tomorrow from this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 21st day of November, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.02 p.m.,
